-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file outside the working directory, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your turn is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

attachment.cliPrefix: You are Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude, running within the Claude Agent SDK.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request

36	PREPARING CHAMPIONS FOR LIFE 
37	 
38	INTRODUCTION 
39	 
40	Participating in 19 varsity sports, Baylor student-athletes compete at the highest level on the field, on the 
41	court, and in the classroom, consistently ranking among the Big 12’s and nation’s best. Baylor Athletics 
42	stands in support of the university’s important mission to educate men and women for worldwide 
43	leadership and service by integrating academic excellence and Christian commitment within a caring 
44	community. This mission informs our day-to-day efforts through one simple purpose: PREPARE 
45	CHAMPIONS FOR LIFE. 
46	 
47	DEFINING CHAMPIONS 
48	 
49	In the context of athletics, the word “champion” evokes images of a game-winning shot, a feat of physical 
50	strength, or a trophy hoisted high by a victorious team; but it has much deeper roots. One of the earliest 
51	definitions is as “one who fights on behalf of others” (circa 1300), and later “to fight for, defend, or 
52	protect” (circa 1820). 
53	 
54	When we say we will “Prepare Champions for Life,” we are calling to that deeper sense of the word. Each 
55	year, more than 500 student-athletes are on campus representing the GREEN and GOLD. Our job is to 
56	educate and prepare these individuals in all aspects of their life, so they leave Waco with a depth of 
57	understanding of what transforms an individual into a champion. 
58	 
59	No team or individual is successful without a successful process – a championship process. Baylor 
60	Athletics focuses on four key areas of development to ensure our student-athletes receive the training 
61	and support we are uniquely equipped to provide. 
62	 
63	Our championship process rests on these four pillars: 
64	• ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT 
65	• ATHLETIC SUCCESS 
66	• SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY 
67	• SPIRITUAL GROWTH

73	ONE STANDARD. ONE ACORD. 
74	 
75	Baylor Athletics’ ability to carry out the vision of Preparing Champions for Life hinges on a collective 
76	commitment to live by ONE STANDARD – to faithfully steward the authentic pursuit of competitive 
77	excellence through Christ. In upholding this standard, the department has committed to be in ONE 
78	ACCORD on six scripturally based operating principles and 18 associated core values. 
79	 
80	 
81	We will do our serviceable and personal best. – Ecclesiastes 9:10 
82	Purpose | Perseverance | Preeminence 
83

108	HEALTH & WELLNESS 
109	 
110	 
111	ATHLETICS PERFORMANCE 
112	The mission of Baylor University Athletics Performance is to set the standard for elite preparation, which 
113	will serve as a bridge to life-long student-athlete success while achieving competitive excellence. 
114	 
115	 
116	ATHLETIC MEDICINE 
117	Baylor University Athletic Medicine (BUAM) promotes health and safety in sport while maintaining an 
118	environment focusing on the Christian mission of Baylor University. BUAM’s objective is to serve the 
119	healthcare needs of Baylor student-athletes promptly and precisely to allow them the opportunity to 
120	achieve success in athletics and life. 
121	 
122	 
123	PERFORMANCE NUTRITION 
124	Baylor Performance Nutrition guides the practical execution of evidence-based nutrition strategies to 
125	optimize athletic performance and foster lifelong healthy behaviors. The department provides individual 
126	consultations, hosts team education sessions, evaluates and informs student-athletes about supplements, 
127	performs body composition and bone density assessments, and oversees the student-athlete training 
128	table (Beauchamp Athletics Nutrition Center) and fueling stations. 
129	 
130	 
131	MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES 
132	Baylor Athletics Mental Health Services (AMHS) is dedicated to the growth and development of student-
133	athletes through providing the highest quality mental health care. Mental health professionals are 
134	available to meet with student-athletes to help them deal with a wide variety of issues that may arise 
135	during their collegiate experience. Professional counselors are trained to help student-athletes identify 
136	and change ways of thinking or behaving that are potentially contributing to their distress or impairing 
137	their functioning. AMHS empowers Baylor student-athletes to discuss their personal concerns in a 
138	confidential and nonjudgmental setting.

144	APPLIED PERFORMANCE 
145	 
146	MISSION 
147	 
148	Operating within the Baylor Athletics Health and Wellness Department, BAYLOR APPLIED PERFORMANCE 
149	drives the elite performance of championship-level athletic programs by leveraging science and 
150	technology through education and relationships. In fulfilling this mission, Applied Performance aims to 
151	enable the high-performance team (Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, 
152	Mental Health Services, and sport coaching staffs) to answer team- and/or technology-specific 
153	questions, ask better questions based on presented evidence; and discover new questions. 
154	 
155	OPERATING PRINCIPLES 
156	 
157	Athlete Monitoring and analysis 
158	• Use various objective and subjective measures related to health and performance across each 
159	season phase (pre-season, in-season, post-season, and off-season). 
160	• Provide information that supports the Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine staff to 
161	determine appropriate training and return-to-performance (RTP) periodization with reference to 
162	typical training and competition demands. 
163	 
164	Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance 
165	• Identify sport- and position-specific key performance indicators (KPIs).  
166	• Conduct athlete evaluations for diagnostic screening, performance testing, and KPI threshold 
167	identification. 
168	 
169	Performance Team Collaboration 
170	• Bring together all members of the high-performance team through effective knowledge 
171	dissemination. 
172	• Provide data to inform the decision-making process throughout Health and Wellness. 
173	 
174	Research and Development 
175	• In collaboration with on-campus faculty, conduct internal and external research on the latest 
176	performance technologies and trends within intercollegiate athletics. 
177	• Provide the high-performance team with knowledge to implement best practices for improving 
178	student-athlete performance and minimizing injury risk.

184	TECHNOLOGY OVERVIEW 
185	 
186	Catapult GPS tracking devices measure various forms of athletic workload in field-based 
187	sports (e.g., high-velocity sprint exposures, heart rate, distance covered, and total 
188	number of accelerations and decelerations). 
189	Catapult OpenField Online platform used to access GPS performance analytics and create data 
190	visualizations. 
191	Kitman Labs Athlete management system (AMS) that acts as a central data storage site for 
192	multiple technologies. Allows for scalable data analysis and visualization across 
193	Baylor sport teams. 
194	Perch Camera-based system that utilizes both hardware and software for Velocity Based 
195	Training (VBT) and weight room performance monitoring. 
196	Polar Chest strap heart rate sensor that measures electrical activity of the heart. 
197	Utilized for aerobic performance and recovery, as well as a gauge for activity 
198	intensity. 
199	VALD DynaMo Handheld dynamometer and inclinometer used to assess strength and range of 
200	motion. 
201	VALD ForceDecks Dual, uniaxial force plates that analyze jumps, strength, power, asymmetry, and 
202	more. 
203	VALD ForceFrame Isometric testing device to quantify and train muscle strength in the upper and 
204	lower extremities (e.g., knee flexion, shoulder internal/external rotation) and 
205	measure limb asymmetry. 
206	VALD Hub Online platform that promotes the generation and sharing of reports with 
207	performance team members. 
208	VALD NordBord Hamstring testing device used to quantify and train hamstring strength and 
209	measure limb asymmetry. 
210	VALD SmartSpeed Timing gate system used to measure speed, agility, and reactivity.

378	Preparation and Set-Up 
379	• Ensure the DynaMo device is charged and ready for use. 
380	• Connect the DynaMo device to the tablet or computer via Bluetooth. Make sure the VALD Performance app is installed and 
381	updated on the device. 
382	• Gather any necessary attachments or accessories required for the specific test you plan to conduct. 
383	Participant Registration 
384	• Open the VALD Performance app on the tablet or computer. 
385	• Create a new participant profile if it's the first time the athlete is being tested. Input all necessary details, such as name, date 
386	of birth, sport, and position. 
387	• If the participant is already registered, select their profile from the database. 
388	Device Calibration 
389	• Follow the on-screen instructions to calibrate the DynaMo device. This usually involves zeroing the sensors to ensure accurate 
390	force readings. 
391	• Confirm that the calibration process is complete before proceeding to the testing phase. 
392	Testing Protocol Set-Up 
393	• Select the appropriate testing protocol from the app, such as grip strength, push-pull strength, or other functional 
394	assessments. 
395	• Adjust the device settings to match the specific requirements of the selected protocol (e.g., duration of the test, number of 
396	repetitions). 
397	Participant Positioning 
398	• Instruct the participant on the correct positioning and technique for the test. Ensure they understand the procedure and 
399	expected effort level. 
400	• Position the participant correctly according to the test protocol. This may involve specific body postures or the use of 
401	attachments to the DynaMo device. 
402	Conducting the Test 
403	• Explain the test procedure to the participant, including how to perform the actions and the importance of maximal effort. 
404	• Start the test using the app interface. The participant will then perform the required actions (e.g., maximal grip contraction). 
405	• Monitor the participant’s form and provide encouragement and instructions as needed throughout the test. 
406	Data Collection and Analysis 
407	• Once the test is completed, review the collected data on the app. Key metrics typically include peak force, average force, and 
408	rate of force development.

444	• Assume starting position – Ask the first individual (profile) in the testing queue to assume the starting position on the plates.

448	tested before stopping the recording. 
449	• Stop recording – Click “Stop” button to examine all results. 
450	• Review – Review and edit results as required. 
451	• Save – Click “Save” to select reps, apply tags and notes; or click “Save All” to save.

819	o Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) is a set of metrics that measures athlete micro movements and direction 
820	regardless of unit orientation. Athlete movements can be quantified into low, medium and high intensity athlete 
821	movements zones that are used to construct profiles of athletes’ movements and to recognize biomechanical red 
822	flags.  
823	o IMA gives indoor and outdoor sports the ability to track acceleration count, deceleration count, asymmetrical 
824	loading, change of direction (COD) count – left and right, free running event count, free running total time, average 
825	stride rate, impacts, and jump count. 
826	o IMA allows the end user to collect and analyze acceleration- and deceleration-based data without the use of a GPS 
827	system. It is beneficial for indoor sessions in which a user cannot collect GPS data. It is also beneficial for breaking 
828	down movements into micro movements which can further be analyzed for performance insights. 
829	 
830	 
831	 
832	3D Position 
833	• Perch uses a 3D camera to directly measure the position of objects in the field of view of the camera. Every image that the 
834	Perch camera captures contains information about how far away objects are from the camera itself. 
835	• Using a complex tracking pipeline developed by engineers at Perch, the camera processes the image to find the objects we’re 
836	interested in (namely, a barbell, parts of the body, etc.). Once the object is located in the image, the device will use the distance 
837	data from the 3D camera and some geometry to triangulate where the object is in 3D space. Otherwise known as determining 
838	the 3D coordinate of the object for this particular point in time. 
839	• 3D position, as its name suggests, consists of three spatial dimensions. The names we use for these dimensions are X, Y, and Z. 
840	We define Z as up and down (parallel to gravity), X as forwards and backwards (in the perspective of the athlete), and Y 
841	as side to side (in the perspective of the athlete). 
842	 
843	3D Path 
844	• The 3D path of an object – in our case, usually a barbell – is nothing more than a sequence of 3D coordinates with time 
845	stamps. By processing images rapidly as the 3D camera captures them, we collect many 3D coordinates and collect them 
846	together to form a 3D path. 
847	• The 3D path represents precisely where in 3D space an object moved over time. This is the core data that Perch captures, 
848	and every other metric is calculated using this 3D path. 
849	 
850	Displacement 
851	• Displacement is simply calculated by subtracting a starting 3D position and from an ending position. If you isolate only one 
852	of the axes, for example the Z axis, you then have the vertical displacement between those positions. For example, in the case 
853	of a back squat, the displacement on the Z axis can be interpreted as the squat depth. 
854	 
855	Velocity 
856	• The equation for velocity is always the same: displacement (aka. distance) divided by time. Since we are able to go from 3D 
857	position to 3D Path and finally calculate displacement, we’re halfway there. Every 3D coordinate also has a corresponding time 
858	associated with it, and we can subtract the times starting and ending 3D coordinates to calculate the amount of time elapsed 
859	between those two positions. 
860	• By dividing the displacement by the time that elapsed between them, you are calculating velocity. 
861	 
862	 
863	 
864	Mean Velocity
865	
866	<!-- page 21 -->
867	14 
868	 
869	 
870	• Mean velocity (or average velocity) as used in VBT is defined as the average velocity of a complete movement (e.g. the 
871	concentric portion of a rep). 
872	• Calculating mean velocity is exactly the same as calculating any other velocity, except the start and end 3D positions you 
873	choose are the beginning and end of the movement respectively. 
874	• For example, to calculate the concentric mean velocity (on the Z axis) of a rep, we perform three calculations: 
875	o We subtract the Z value of the coordinate of the bottom of the rep (the beginning of the concentric movement) from 
876	the highest point at the end of the rep (the final coordinate of the concentric movement) to calculate the 
877	displacement. 
878	o We subtract the times of the same two coordinates chosen above to calculate the duration of the concentric 
879	movement. 
880	o Finally, we divide the displacement by the duration to get the velocity. 
881	• Concentric and Eccentric Mean Velocity are both captured in the system and are registered separately – one will not impact 
882	the other. 
883	 
884	Peak Velocity 
885	• Calculating peak velocity is once again very similar to other velocity calculations, however it differs in selection of the 
886	coordinates. 
887	• Peak velocity is defined as the greatest instantaneous velocity during a movement. Here, “instantaneous” means between 
888	two consecutive coordinates. Naturally, there is some amount of time between each coordinate we measure, so using two 
889	adjacent coordinates is not truly instantaneous, but is sufficiently close. 
890	• As an example, to find the peak concentric velocity (on the Z axis), we do the following: 
891	o Compute the instantaneous velocity using every pair of consecutive coordinates from the lowest to the highest point 
892	of the movement (following the same procedure as defined above) 
893	o The largest of these instantaneous velocities is your peak concentric velocity 
894	 
895	Eccentric Time 
896	• Eccentric time is tracking the amount of time, in seconds, it takes to complete the eccentric portion of the movement. This is 
897	not displayed on the tablet for Olympic lifts or for jumps. 
898	• We subtract the Z value of the coordinate of the top of the rep (the beginning of the eccentric movement) from the lowest point 
899	at the end of the rep (the final coordinate of the eccentric movement). We subtract the times of the same two coordinates to 
900	calculate the duration of the eccentric movement. 
901	 
902	Power 
903	• The equation for power is defined as Work divided by time: P = W / t 
904	• In our case, the force is how much force the athlete is applying to the barbell. While we’ve already covered how we can 
905	calculate velocity (the Vterm), we can’t directly measure the force. However, we can calculate it in a couple different ways 
906	depending on the context. 
907	 
908	Mean Power 
909	• Mean power can be described as the average amount of power over the duration of the movement. To calculate, we can 
910	reuse the mean velocity we’ve already calculated above for the V term in our power equations. 
911	• The force (F) in our equation is similarly the average force applied by the athlete during the movement. Because the bar is 
912	at rest before and after the movement, the average force is equal to the force required to oppose gravity (aka, the force of 
913	gravity) on the barbell. As such, the force is the mass of the barbell (in kilograms) multiplied by the acceleration due to 
914	gravity (9.8 m/s). 
915	• With the math established, calculating mean power is as simple as substituting the mass of the barbell (converted to 
916	kilograms, m) and the mean velocity (in meters per second, V) into the following equation: Mean Power = m x 9.8 x V 
917	 
918	Peak Power
919	
920	<!-- page 22 -->
921	15 
922	 
923	 
924	• Calculating peak power requires a bit more complexity, as was the case with peak velocity. 
925	• In order to calculate the peak power output for a movement, we calculate the instantaneous power at every point during 
926	the movement and select the largest. 
927	• Here is the general procedure for how we calculate peak power for a concentric movement: 
928	o Using the same procedure as in peak velocity, calculate the instantaneous velocity for every pair of points in the 
929	movement. 
930	o Using every consecutive pair of instantaneous velocities computed in the previous step, compute the instantaneous 
931	acceleration (acceleration is change in velocity divided by time). 
932	o For each instantaneous measurement of velocity and acceleration, plug in the following variables. 
933	 The instantaneous acceleration (a) 
934	 The instantaneous velocity (v) 
935	 The weight in kilograms of the barbell (m) 
936	• Peak Power = m x a x V 
937	• Select the largest value; this is your peak power. 
938	 
939	Work 
940	• As we referenced in the sections discussing Power, Work can be calculated as W = Fd, where F is the average force applied by 
941	the athlete to the barbell and d is the displacement of the movement. Work is presented in units of Kilojoules (kJ), which is a 
942	measure of Energy. Work can be thought of as the amount of energy the athlete put into the barbell by lifting it against gravity. 
943	 
944	Time to Peak Power (T2PP) 
945	• Based on the calculation for Peak Power above (Peak Power = m x a x V), the time to peak power is the duration in seconds it 
946	takes to achieve that peak power, based on the start of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as T2PP as an 
947	abbreviation in the app. 
948	 
949	Time to Peak Velocity (T2PV) 
950	• Based on the calculation for Peak Velocity above, the time to peak velocity is the duration in seconds it takes to achieve that 
951	peak velocity, based on the start of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as T2PV as an abbreviation in the app. 
952	 
953	Velocity at 100ms (V100) 
954	• The v100 is a new metric that will help to track explosiveness of athletes, among other things.  This is based similarly to 
955	calculations above of time to peak velocity and power, but instead measures the velocity at which the bar is moving within the 
956	first 100 milliseconds of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as V100 as an abbreviation in the app. 
957	 
958	Jump Assessment Concepts 
959	• Jump assessments have special metrics calculated specifically for them. These metrics are built  off of the same tracking 
960	technology used for other exercises. Here's what you need to know. 
961	 
962	Types of Jumping 
963	• Counter Movement Jump (CMJ) 
964	o A counter movement jump is defined in Perch as a jump where the athlete begins by standing up straight, dips into a 
965	preload by bending knees and hips to a self-selected depth, and then rapidly explodes out of their preload into a 
966	vertical jump as high as possible. 
967	o When performing multiple repetitions, the athlete should land from their previous jump, reset, and return to their 
968	original standing position before beginning their next jump. 
969	• Continuous Jumps 
970	o A continuous jumping exercise starts similarly to a counter movement jump. The athlete will stand up straight before 
971	preloading to a self-selected depth, and then explode into their first repetition of a vertical jump.
972	
973	<!-- page 23 -->
974	16 
975	 
976	 
977	o However, instead of landing and pausing to return to a standing position, the athlete’s landing from the previous 
978	jump flows smoothly into the preload of their next jump. Thus, the athlete performs multiple jumps without rest in 
979	between. A priority should be minimizing ground contact time while maximizing jump height. 
980	• Tracking a Jump 
981	o Because Perch measures 3D position of objects, we track the position of parts of the athlete’s body to 
982	track jumps and other non-barbell exercises. The primary object used for tracking jumps is the athlete’s 
983	head. 
984	o To track a jump, Perch uses the position of the athlete's head right before beginning their jump to measure 
985	their standing height. When the athlete begins unweighting, for either a CMJ or Continuous Jumps, that 
986	marks the beginning of the jump. 
987	o For continuous jumps, the beginning of each repetition after the athlete’s first is the same as the moment 
988	the athlete lands from the previous repetition. 
989	o After preloading, the athlete explodes upwards into their jump (the propulsive phase). The moment the 
990	athlete returns to their original starting height (the end of the propulsive phase) is defined as the moment 
991	of takeoff. The athlete’s feet will leave the ground at this moment in time. 
992	o During the jump, the athlete rises and falls in the air (the flight phase). The apex of the jump can be 
993	measured as the highest point the athlete reaches after takeoff. The moment the athlete lands is the 
994	moment when the athlete falls back to their original standing height, before decelerating and absorbing the 
995	landing. 
996	• Jump Height 
997	o Jump height is a measure of displacement. Given the above definitions, Perch measures 
998	jump height simply by subtracting the height of the apex of the jump from the athlete’s 
999	standing height before the beginning of the jump. 
1000	• Time to Takeoff 
1001	o Time to takeoff is measured as the amount of time elapsed between the beginning of the 
1002	jump (the start of the unweighting phase) until the moment of takeoff (the end of the 
1003	propulsive phase). 
1004	o This time includes the full duration of the following jump phases: 
1005	 Unweighting 
1006	 Braking 
1007	 Propulsive 
1008	• Takeoff Velocity 
1009	o Takeoff velocity is a measure of instantaneous velocity at the moment of takeoff (the end of the propulsive 
1010	phase). This is the speed at which the athlete is moving just before their feet leave the ground after the 
1011	propulsive phase. 
1012	• RSIMod 
1013	o RSIMod is Jump Height divided by Time to Takeoff. It is reported as a unitless quantity, rather than its true 
1014	unit of m/s, since it should not be interpreted as a velocity.

PREPARING CHAMPIONS FOR LIFE 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Participating in 19 varsity sports, Baylor student-athletes compete at the highest level on the field, on the 
court, and in the classroom, consistently ranking among the Big 12’s and nation’s best. Baylor Athletics 
stands in support of the university’s important mission to educate men and women for worldwide 
leadership and service by integrating academic excellence and Christian commitment within a caring 
community. This mission informs our day-to-day efforts through one simple purpose: PREPARE 
CHAMPIONS FOR LIFE. 
 
DEFINING CHAMPIONS 
 
In the context of athletics, the word “champion” evokes images of a game-winning shot, a feat of physical 
strength, or a trophy hoisted high by a victorious team; but it has much deeper roots. One of the earliest 
definitions is as “one who fights on behalf of others” (circa 1300), and later “to fight for, defend, or 
protect” (circa 1820). 
 
When we say we will “Prepare Champions for Life,” we are calling to that deeper sense of the word. Each 
year, more than 500 student-athletes are on campus representing the GREEN and GOLD. Our job is to 
educate and prepare these individuals in all aspects of their life, so they leave Waco with a depth of 
understanding of what transforms an individual into a champion. 
 
No team or individual is successful without a successful process – a championship process. Baylor 
Athletics focuses on four key areas of development to ensure our student-athletes receive the training 
and support we are uniquely equipped to provide. 
 
Our championship process rests on these four pillars: 
• ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT 
• ATHLETIC SUCCESS 
• SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY 
• SPIRITUAL GROWTH

<!-- page 4 -->
4 
 
 
ONE STANDARD. ONE ACORD. 
 
Baylor Athletics’ ability to carry out the vision of Preparing Champions for Life hinges on a collective 
commitment to live by ONE STANDARD – to faithfully steward the authentic pursuit of competitive 
excellence through Christ. In upholding this standard, the department has committed to be in ONE 
ACCORD on six scripturally based operating principles and 18 associated core values. 
 
 
We will do our serviceable and personal best. – Ecclesiastes 9:10 
Purpose | Perseverance | Preeminence 
 
 
We will commit to principled innovation. – Romans 12:2 
Reflection | Aspiration | Advancement 
 
 
We will master fundamentals and pursue excellence. – Ephesians 2:10 
Intent | Equip | Championships 
 
 
We will treat one another with dignity and respect. – Colossians 3:12-14 
Service | Love | Truth 
 
 
We will welcome vulnerability and accountability. – Psalm 139:23-24 
Inclusivity | Humility | Trust 
 
 
We will make all decisions in accordance with governing regulations. – Galatians 6:9 
Virtue | Transparent | Vigilance

<!-- page 5 -->
5 
 
 
HEALTH & WELLNESS 
 
 
ATHLETICS PERFORMANCE 
The mission of Baylor University Athletics Performance is to set the standard for elite preparation, which 
will serve as a bridge to life-long student-athlete success while achieving competitive excellence. 
 
 
ATHLETIC MEDICINE 
Baylor University Athletic Medicine (BUAM) promotes health and safety in sport while maintaining an 
environment focusing on the Christian mission of Baylor University. BUAM’s objective is to serve the 
healthcare needs of Baylor student-athletes promptly and precisely to allow them the opportunity to 
achieve success in athletics and life. 
 
 
PERFORMANCE NUTRITION 
Baylor Performance Nutrition guides the practical execution of evidence-based nutrition strategies to 
optimize athletic performance and foster lifelong healthy behaviors. The department provides individual 
consultations, hosts team education sessions, evaluates and informs student-athletes about supplements, 
performs body composition and bone density assessments, and oversees the student-athlete training

DATA DICTIONARY 
 
 
 
Basic Parameters 
• Maximum Velocity – maximum velocity reached, dependent on time interval selected (period/session) 
• Total Distance – total distance covered during selected time interval (periods/sessions)  
• Player Load – Total Player Load accumulated during time interval selected; measures an athlete’s physical effort during movement 
• Field Time – the total amount of time an athlete is interchanged “IN” during activities 
• Heart Rate – Instantaneous Heart Rate (BPM); value for a Period is the last recorded instantaneous Heart Rate (BPM)  
• Max Heart Rate – Maximum Heart Rate (BPM) dependent on time interval selected (period/session) 
• Mean Heart Rate – Average Heart Rate (BPM) dependent on time interval selected (period/session) 
• Distance Per Minute – average meters/yards covered per minute, dependent on time interval selected (period/session)  
• Device ID – the ID of the Vector Device worn by the athlete 
• Position Name – position defined by athlete in database 
Heart Rate Parameters 
• Heart Rate – Instantaneous Heart Rate (BPM). Value for a period is the lost recorded instantaneous Heart Rate (BPM) 
• Maximum Heart Rate – Maximum Heart Rate (BPM) dependent on time interval selected (period/session) 
• Mean Heart Rate – Average Heart Rate (BPM) dependent on time interval selected (period/session) 
• Heart Rate Duration Bands – tap to select a band to view the total duration spent while within the selected heart rate band  
• Percentage Heart Rate Max – Instantaneous Heart Rate as a percentage of an athlete's max heart rate; value for a period is the last 
recorded instantaneous Heart Rate (BPM) 
• Heart Rate Red Zone Minutes – total accumulated duration spent while within the selected heart rate bands; tap to select the bands you 
want to include in the calculation 
Velocity Parameters 
• Maximum Velocity – Maximum Velocity reached, dependent on time interval selected (period/session) 
• Velocity Duration Bands – tap to select a band to view the total duration spent while within the selected velocity band 
• Velocity Distance Bands – tap to select a band to view the total distance accumulated while within the selected velocity band 
• Velocity Effort Bands – tap to select a band to view the total amount of times the specified velocity band was reached  
• Velocity Distance Bands (Set 2) – tap to select a band to view the total distance accumulated while within the selected velocity band  
• Velocity Effort Bands (Set 2) – tap to select a band to view the total amount of times the specified velocity band was reached  
• Maximum Velocity (% Max) – Maximum Velocity for an activity or period as a percentage of an athlete's profile max velocity 
Acceleration Parameters 
• Deceleration Effort Bands – tap to select a band to view the total amount of times an athlete reached the selected deceleration band (as 
defined by dwell time) 
• Acceleration Effort Bands – tap to select a band to view the total amount of times an athlete reached the selected acceleration band (as 
defined by dwell time)

• Acceleration Bands 1-3 Effort – the total amount of times an athlete accelerated. An accumulation of Acceleration Bands 1, 2 and 3 (as 
defined by dwell time) 
• Acceleration Bands 2-3 Effort – the total amount of times an athlete accelerated within Acceleration Bands 2 and 3 (as defined by dwell 
time) 
• Deceleration Bands 1-3 Effort – the total amount of times an athlete decelerated. An accumulation of Deceleration Bands 1, 2 and 3 (as 
defined by dwell time) 
• Deceleration Bands 2-3 Effort – the total amount of times an athlete decelerated within Deceleration Bands 2 and 3 (as defined by dwell 
time) 
Player Load Parameters 
• Player Load – Total Player Load accumulated during time interval selected 
• Player Load Per Minute – Average Player Load accumulated per minute during time interval selected (period/session)  
• Player Load Bands – tap to select a band to view the total Player Load accumulated while within the selected Player Load band  
• Player Load Duration Bands – tap to select a band to view the total duration spent while within the selected Player Load band

• Very High Speed Effort – total number of velocity efforts while within the selected velocity bands. Tap to select the bands you 
want to include in the calculation 
• Very High Speed Effort Percentage – Very High Speed Effort as a percentage of Total Efforts 
• Very High Intensity Player Load Duration – total accumulated duration while within the selected Player Load bands. Tap to 
select the bands you want to include in the calculation 
• Very High Intensity Player Load Duration Percentage – total accumulated duration as a percentage of Total Duration 
• Very High Intensity Player Load – total accumulated Player Load while within the selected Player Load bands. Tap to select 
the bands you want to include in the calculation 
• Very High Intensity Player Load Percentage – Very High Player Load as a percentage of Total Player Load 
Other 
• IMA

<!-- page 20 -->
13 
 
 
o Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) is a set of metrics that measures athlete micro movements and direction 
regardless of unit orientation. Athlete movements can be quantified into low, medium and high intensity athlete 
movements zones that are used to construct profiles of athletes’ movements and to recognize biomechanical red 
flags.  
o IMA gives indoor and outdoor sports the ability to track acceleration count, deceleration count, asymmetrical 
loading, change of direction (COD) count – left and right, free running event count, free running total time, average 
stride rate, impacts, and jump count. 
o IMA allows the end user to collect and analyze acceleration- and deceleration-based data without the use of a GPS 
system. It is beneficial for indoor sessions in which a user cannot collect GPS data. It is also beneficial for breaking 
down movements into micro movements which can further be analyzed for performance insights. 
 
 
 
3D Position 
• Perch uses a 3D camera to directly measure the position of objects in the field of view of the camera. Every image that the 
Perch camera captures contains information about how far away objects are from the camera itself. 
• Using a complex tracking pipeline developed by engineers at Perch, the camera processes the image to find the objects we’re 
interested in (namely, a barbell, parts of the body, etc.). Once the object is located in the image, the device will use the distance 
data from the 3D camera and some geometry to triangulate where the object is in 3D space. Otherwise known as determining 
the 3D coordinate of the object for this particular point in time. 
• 3D position, as its name suggests, consists of three spatial dimensions. The names we use for these dimensions are X, Y, and Z. 
We define Z as up and down (parallel to gravity), X as forwards and backwards (in the perspective of the athlete), and Y 
as side to side (in the perspective of the athlete). 
 
3D Path 
• The 3D path of an object – in our case, usually a barbell – is nothing more than a sequence of 3D coordinates with time 
stamps. By processing images rapidly as the 3D camera captures them, we collect many 3D coordinates and collect them 
together to form a 3D path. 
• The 3D path represents precisely where in 3D space an object moved over time. This is the core data that Perch captures, 
and every other metric is calculated using this 3D path. 
 
Displacement 
• Displacement is simply calculated by subtracting a starting 3D position and from an ending position. If you isolate only one 
of the axes, for example the Z axis, you then have the vertical displacement between those positions. For example, in the case 
of a back squat, the displacement on the Z axis can be interpreted as the squat depth. 
 
Velocity 
• The equation for velocity is always the same: displacement (aka. distance) divided by time. Since we are able to go from 3D 
position to 3D Path and finally calculate displacement, we’re halfway there. Every 3D coordinate also has a corresponding time 
associated with it, and we can subtract the times starting and ending 3D coordinates to calculate the amount of time elapsed 
between those two positions. 
• By dividing the displacement by the time that elapsed between them, you are calculating velocity. 
 
 
 
Mean Velocity

<!-- page 21 -->
14 
 
 
• Mean velocity (or average velocity) as used in VBT is defined as the average velocity of a complete movement (e.g. the 
concentric portion of a rep). 
• Calculating mean velocity is exactly the same as calculating any other velocity, except the start and end 3D positions you 
choose are the beginning and end of the movement respectively. 
• For example, to calculate the concentric mean velocity (on the Z axis) of a rep, we perform three calculations: 
o We subtract the Z value of the coordinate of the bottom of the rep (the beginning of the concentric movement) from 
the highest point at the end of the rep (the final coordinate of the concentric movement) to calculate the 
displacement. 
o We subtract the times of the same two coordinates chosen above to calculate the duration of the concentric 
movement. 
o Finally, we divide the displacement by the duration to get the velocity. 
• Concentric and Eccentric Mean Velocity are both captured in the system and are registered separately – one will not impact 
the other. 
 
Peak Velocity 
• Calculating peak velocity is once again very similar to other velocity calculations, however it differs in selection of the 
coordinates. 
• Peak velocity is defined as the greatest instantaneous velocity during a movement. Here, “instantaneous” means between 
two consecutive coordinates. Naturally, there is some amount of time between each coordinate we measure, so using two 
adjacent coordinates is not truly instantaneous, but is sufficiently close. 
• As an example, to find the peak concentric velocity (on the Z axis), we do the following: 
o Compute the instantaneous velocity using every pair of consecutive coordinates from the lowest to the highest point 
of the movement (following the same procedure as defined above) 
o The largest of these instantaneous velocities is your peak concentric velocity 
 
Eccentric Time 
• Eccentric time is tracking the amount of time, in seconds, it takes to complete the eccentric portion of the movement. This is 
not displayed on the tablet for Olympic lifts or for jumps. 
• We subtract the Z value of the coordinate of the top of the rep (the beginning of the eccentric movement) from the lowest point 
at the end of the rep (the final coordinate of the eccentric movement). We subtract the times of the same two coordinates to 
calculate the duration of the eccentric movement. 
 
Power 
• The equation for power is defined as Work divided by time: P = W / t 
• In our case, the force is how much force the athlete is applying to the barbell. While we’ve already covered how we can 
calculate velocity (the Vterm), we can’t directly measure the force. However, we can calculate it in a couple different ways 
depending on the context. 
 
Mean Power 
• Mean power can be described as the average amount of power over the duration of the movement. To calculate, we can 
reuse the mean velocity we’ve already calculated above for the V term in our power equations. 
• The force (F) in our equation is similarly the average force applied by the athlete during the movement. Because the bar is 
at rest before and after the movement, the average force is equal to the force required to oppose gravity (aka, the force of 
gravity) on the barbell. As such, the force is the mass of the barbell (in kilograms) multiplied by the acceleration due to 
gravity (9.8 m/s). 
• With the math established, calculating mean power is as simple as substituting the mass of the barbell (converted to 
kilograms, m) and the mean velocity (in meters per second, V) into the following equation: Mean Power = m x 9.8 x V 
 
Peak Power

<!-- page 22 -->
15 
 
 
• Calculating peak power requires a bit more complexity, as was the case with peak velocity. 
• In order to calculate the peak power output for a movement, we calculate the instantaneous power at every point during 
the movement and select the largest. 
• Here is the general procedure for how we calculate peak power for a concentric movement: 
o Using the same procedure as in peak velocity, calculate the instantaneous velocity for every pair of points in the 
movement. 
o Using every consecutive pair of instantaneous velocities computed in the previous step, compute the instantaneous 
acceleration (acceleration is change in velocity divided by time). 
o For each instantaneous measurement of velocity and acceleration, plug in the following variables. 
 The instantaneous acceleration (a) 
 The instantaneous velocity (v) 
 The weight in kilograms of the barbell (m) 
• Peak Power = m x a x V 
• Select the largest value; this is your peak power. 
 
Work 
• As we referenced in the sections discussing Power, Work can be calculated as W = Fd, where F is the average force applied by 
the athlete to the barbell and d is the displacement of the movement. Work is presented in units of Kilojoules (kJ), which is a 
measure of Energy. Work can be thought of as the amount of energy the athlete put into the barbell by lifting it against gravity. 
 
Time to Peak Power (T2PP) 
• Based on the calculation for Peak Power above (Peak Power = m x a x V), the time to peak power is the duration in seconds it 
takes to achieve that peak power, based on the start of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as T2PP as an 
abbreviation in the app. 
 
Time to Peak Velocity (T2PV) 
• Based on the calculation for Peak Velocity above, the time to peak velocity is the duration in seconds it takes to achieve that 
peak velocity, based on the start of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as T2PV as an abbreviation in the app. 
 
Velocity at 100ms (V100) 
• The v100 is a new metric that will help to track explosiveness of athletes, among other things.  This is based similarly to 
calculations above of time to peak velocity and power, but instead measures the velocity at which the bar is moving within the 
first 100 milliseconds of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as V100 as an abbreviation in the app. 
 
Jump Assessment Concepts 
• Jump assessments have special metrics calculated specifically for them. These metrics are built  off of the same tracking 
technology used for other exercises. Here's what you need to know. 
 
Types of Jumping 
• Counter Movement Jump (CMJ) 
o A counter movement jump is defined in Perch as a jump where the athlete begins by standing up straight, dips into a 
preload by bending knees and hips to a self-selected depth, and then rapidly explodes out of their preload into a 
vertical jump as high as possible. 
o When performing multiple repetitions, the athlete should land from their previous jump, reset, and return to their 
original standing position before beginning their next jump. 
• Continuous Jumps 
o A continuous jumping exercise starts similarly to a counter movement jump. The athlete will stand up straight before 
preloading to a self-selected depth, and then explode into their first repetition of a vertical jump.

<!-- page 23 -->
16 
 
 
o However, instead of landing and pausing to return to a standing position, the athlete’s landing from the previous 
jump flows smoothly into the preload of their next jump. Thus, the athlete performs multiple jumps without rest in 
between. A priority should be minimizing ground contact time while maximizing jump height. 
• Tracking a Jump 
o Because Perch measures 3D position of objects, we track the position of parts of the athlete’s body to 
track jumps and other non-barbell exercises. The primary object used for tracking jumps is the athlete’s 
head. 
o To track a jump, Perch uses the position of the athlete's head right before beginning their jump to measure 
their standing height. When the athlete begins unweighting, for either a CMJ or Continuous Jumps, that 
marks the beginning of the jump. 
o For continuous jumps, the beginning of each repetition after the athlete’s first is the same as the moment 
the athlete lands from the previous repetition. 
o After preloading, the athlete explodes upwards into their jump (the propulsive phase). The moment the 
athlete returns to their original starting height (the end of the propulsive phase) is defined as the moment 
of takeoff. The athlete’s feet will leave the ground at this moment in time. 
o During the jump, the athlete rises and falls in the air (the flight phase). The apex of the jump can be 
measured as the highest point the athlete reaches after takeoff. The moment the athlete lands is the 
moment when the athlete falls back to their original standing height, before decelerating and absorbing the 
landing. 
• Jump Height 
o Jump height is a measure of displacement. Given the above definitions, Perch measures 
jump height simply by subtracting the height of the apex of the jump from the athlete’s 
standing height before the beginning of the jump. 
• Time to Takeoff 
o Time to takeoff is measured as the amount of time elapsed between the beginning of the 
jump (the start of the unweighting phase) until the moment of takeoff (the end of the 
propulsive phase). 
o This time includes the full duration of the following jump phases: 
 Unweighting 
 Braking 
 Propulsive 
• Takeoff Velocity 
o Takeoff velocity is a measure of instantaneous velocity at the moment of takeoff (the end of the propulsive 
phase). This is the speed at which the athlete is moving just before their feet leave the ground after the 
propulsive phase. 
• RSIMod 
o RSIMod is Jump Height divided by Time to Takeoff. It is reported as a unitless quantity, rather than its true 
unit of m/s, since it should not be interpreted as a velocity.

<!-- page 24 -->
17

7	BAYLOR ATHLETICS
8	
9	PERFORMANCE PLAYBOOK
10	
11	Development Plan & Gap Analysis
12	
13	Comparative Review: Clemson OLY Sports Science Playbook vs. Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide
14	
15	Including: Intern Sport Science Curriculum Framework (NSCA CPSS-Aligned)
16	
17	February 2026
18	
19	## SECTION 1: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
20	
21	This document provides a comprehensive gap analysis comparing the Clemson Olympic Sports Science Playbook (Spring 2023) with the current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide. It identifies structural, content, and strategic differences between the two documents and delivers a prioritized action plan for developing the Baylor Performance Playbook into a best-in-class departmental training and SOP manual. Additionally, it outlines a standalone Intern Sport Science Curriculum aligned with the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook.
22	
23	### Key Findings
24	
25	The Baylor document is a solid operational foundation but is significantly less comprehensive than the Clemson model. The primary gaps fall into five categories:
26	
27	No intern/GA curriculum or educational programming structure
28	
29	No sport-specific data dictionaries (the current data dictionary is generic/vendor-level, not contextualized to Baylor sports)
30	
31	Missing daily operational checklists, schedules, and accountability structures
32	
33	Technology workflows are generic and template-like rather than Baylor-specific with step-by-step detail
34	
35	No guiding principles, policies, or professional development framework for staff and interns
36	
37	## SECTION 2: STRUCTURAL COMPARISON
38	
39	The following table maps the major sections of each document to highlight what exists, what is missing, and what needs development.
40	
41	## SECTION 3: DETAILED CRITIQUE OF THE BAYLOR OPERATIONS GUIDE
42	
43	### 3.1 Strengths
44	
45	Strong institutional framing: The Preparing Champions for Life mission and One Standard/One Accord values provide a meaningful organizational identity that Clemson lacks.
46	
47	Health & Wellness ecosystem: The inclusion of Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services missions establishes Applied Performance within the broader support structure.
48	
49	ForceDecks data dictionary depth: The jump metric glossary (take-off phase, landing phase metrics) is more technically detailed than Clemson's equivalent.
50	
51	Perch VBT metric explanations: The 3D position, velocity, and power calculation breakdowns are well-written and educationally valuable.
52	
53	Hyperlinked resources: External links to vendor user manuals and test guides add value without bloating the document.
54	
55	### 3.2 Weaknesses & Gaps
56	
57	#### 3.2.1 Identity and Purpose
58	
59	The Baylor document reads more like a vendor product reference manual than a departmental playbook. The Clemson document tells you who they are, what they do, and why it matters before presenting any technology. The Baylor version jumps from institutional mission directly into technology with very little connecting tissue explaining how Applied Performance operates day-to-day.
60	
61	#### 3.2.2 Technology Workflows
62	
63	The VALD DynaMo, ForceFrame, NordBord, Perch, Polar, and SmartSpeed workflows all follow an identical template structure (Preparation, Participant Registration, Device Calibration, Testing Protocol, Positioning, Conducting the Test, Data Collection, Feedback, Post-Test, Data Export). While organized, this template-driven approach has several problems:
64	
65	It reads like it was generated from a generic template rather than written from practitioner experience at Baylor.
66	
67	There are no Baylor-specific device names, serial numbers, storage locations, or account details.
68	
69	There is no troubleshooting section for any device (Clemson includes troubleshooting for every technology).
70	
71	The Catapult workflow is the only one with genuine operational detail; the others need the same treatment.
72	
73	#### 3.2.3 Data Dictionary
74	
75	The current data dictionary is organized by technology vendor (Catapult parameters, Perch parameters, ForceDecks parameters, Polar parameters) rather than by sport. This means a staff member working with soccer cannot quickly find all the metrics relevant to their team. Clemson organizes their data dictionary by sport (Baseball, Men's Soccer, Volleyball, etc.) and lists only the technologies and metrics used by each sport. This is far more actionable for coaches and performance staff.
76	
77	#### 3.2.4 Missing Operational Infrastructure
78	
79	The following operational elements are entirely absent from the Baylor document:
80	
81	Daily intern/GA checklist with device charging and readiness protocols
82	
83	Social media and student-athlete interaction policies
84	
85	Intern/GA schedule and semester learning objectives
86	
87	Professional expectations and conduct standards
88	
89	Data management and reporting pipelines (where does data go after collection?)
90	
91	Credential and password management protocol
92	
93	Equipment maintenance schedule and inventory tracking
94	
95	#### 3.2.5 Educational and Development Components
96	
97	The Clemson Playbook doubles as a training manual. It includes a 173-page intern curriculum with slide-deck-style educational content covering the fundamentals of sports science, force plates, GPS, force-velocity profiling, heart rate monitoring, data hygiene, data visualization, soft skills, research methods, sports medicine, and strength & conditioning. The Baylor document has no educational component whatsoever. Any intern or new staff member receiving the Baylor document would know how to set up devices but would not understand why they are doing so or how the data fits into the bigger picture.
98	
99	## SECTION 4: PRIORITIZED ACTION PLAN
100	
101	The following action plan is organized into three phases based on impact and effort.
102	
103	### Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1–4)
104	
105	High-impact, relatively low-effort additions that immediately improve the document's utility.
106	
107	Draft an Applied Performance Introduction section that explains who the team is, what interns/GAs can expect, and daily responsibilities.
108	
109	Create a Policies section covering social media, student-athlete interactions, confidentiality, and professional conduct.
110	
111	Build a Daily Operations Checklist with device inventory, charging protocols, pre-session setup, and post-session teardown tasks.
112	
113	Expand the Operating Principles from bullet format to narrative descriptions with practical examples.
114	
115	Establish a credential management protocol (e.g., shared 1Password vault) and document the process in the Playbook.
116	
117	### Phase 2: Operational Depth (Weeks 5–10)
118	
119	Moderate-effort improvements that transform the document from a reference guide into a true operational playbook.
120	
121	Rewrite all technology workflows with Baylor-specific details: device names/serial numbers, storage locations, account credentials (referenced via vault), step-by-step procedures written from practitioner experience, and troubleshooting guides.
122	
123	Create sport-specific data dictionaries for each team supported by Applied Performance, listing only the technologies and KPIs relevant to that sport with contextualized threshold values.
124	
125	Develop a data management pipeline section documenting the flow from data collection through storage (Kitman Labs, VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud), analysis, visualization, and reporting.
126	
127	Add an Equipment Inventory and Maintenance section with serial numbers, purchase dates, warranty info, and maintenance schedules.
128	
129	Create reporting templates and dashboards section showing examples of weekly/monthly reports for coaching staffs.
130	
131	### Phase 3: Education & Culture (Weeks 11–16+)
132	
133	Higher-effort additions that elevate the Playbook into a comprehensive training and development resource.
134	
135	Develop the standalone Intern Sport Science Curriculum (see Section 5 below).
136	
137	Create an Intern/GA Semester Schedule with weekly topics, learning objectives, deliverables, and presentation milestones.
138	
139	Build a Professional Development section with networking expectations, conference attendance, social media best practices, and career pathway guidance.
140	
141	Add case studies and applied practice scenarios for each technology/sport combination to bridge the gap between data collection and decision-making.
142	
143	Establish a version control and review cycle (e.g., annual review each May with updates before fall semester).
144	
145	## SECTION 5: INTERN SPORT SCIENCE CURRICULUM FRAMEWORK
146	
147	The following outlines a standalone 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum designed to be a separate document from the Performance Playbook. It is aligned with the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook and adapted from the Clemson model to reflect Baylor's technology stack, organizational structure, and operational philosophy.
148	
149	### 5.1 Curriculum Philosophy
150	
151	The curriculum is built on the principle that interns must understand both the why and the how of applied sport science. Each week combines conceptual education (readings, lectures, discussions) with hands-on technical training (device operation, data collection, analysis). Interns should leave the program with a portfolio of work and the confidence to operate independently in a collegiate sport science environment.
152	
153	### 5.2 Semester Schedule
154	
155	### 5.3 Key Differences from the Clemson Curriculum
156	
157	While the Clemson curriculum provides an excellent template, the Baylor version should be adapted in several important ways:
158	
159	Technology alignment: Clemson's curriculum references 1080 Sprint, Proteus, Moxy, MuscleLab, PlyoMat, and GymAware, none of which are in Baylor's current stack. The Baylor curriculum should center on ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, and Polar.
160	
161	Sport context: Clemson's examples lean heavily on Olympic sports (soccer, volleyball, rowing, softball, baseball, track). Baylor should incorporate football-specific examples alongside Olympic sport contexts given the department structure.
162	
163	Standalone format: Clemson embeds the curriculum inside the Playbook as slide decks. Baylor should create a separate, dedicated curriculum document that can be distributed independently and updated on its own cycle.
164	
165	Assessment and portfolio: Add formal intern assessment rubrics and require a portfolio of work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics) that interns can use professionally.
166	
167	Integration with Health & Wellness: Baylor's unique structure (Applied Performance within Health & Wellness) should be reflected in the curriculum by including sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health Services.
168	
169	### 5.4 Intern Project Requirements
170	
171	Each intern should complete a semester-long project that demonstrates applied competency. Suggested project categories:
172	
173	Sport-specific dashboard: Build a weekly or monthly reporting dashboard for one Baylor sport using real (de-identified) data.
174	
175	Technology validation: Conduct a reliability or validity study on a Baylor technology using appropriate statistical methods.
176	
177	Literature review and infographic: Summarize the current evidence on a sport science topic and translate it into a practitioner-facing infographic.
178	
179	Data integration project: Combine data from two or more sources (e.g., GPS + force plates + wellness) and present an integrated analysis.
180	
181	## SECTION 6: RECOMMENDED FINAL PLAYBOOK STRUCTURE
182	
183	Based on this analysis, the completed Baylor Performance Playbook should follow this structure:
184	
185	Note: The Intern Sport Science Curriculum should be maintained as a separate standalone document that references the Playbook but can be distributed and updated independently.
186	
187	## SECTION 7: NEXT STEPS
188	
189	To move from this plan to execution, the following immediate next steps are recommended:
190	
191	Review this document and prioritize which Phase 1 items to tackle first based on upcoming semester needs.
192	
193	Assign ownership for each Playbook section (e.g., who writes the Catapult workflow vs. the ForceDecks workflow).
194	
195	Determine the target completion date for each phase (suggest: Phase 1 complete before fall semester, Phase 2 by mid-fall, Phase 3 by end of fall).
196	
197	Decide on the Intern Curriculum delivery format: separate PDF, slide decks, or a combination.
198	
199	Identify 2–3 sports to pilot the sport-specific data dictionaries and use them as templates for the rest.
200	
201	Establish a shared workspace (e.g., Google Drive folder, SharePoint site) for collaborative editing of the Playbook.
