BAYLOR ATHLETICS

PERFORMANCE PLAYBOOK

Development Plan & Gap Analysis

Comparative Review: Clemson OLY Sports Science Playbook vs. Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide

Including: Intern Sport Science Curriculum Framework (NSCA CPSS-Aligned)

February 2026

## SECTION 1: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This document provides a comprehensive gap analysis comparing the Clemson Olympic Sports Science Playbook (Spring 2023) with the current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide. It identifies structural, content, and strategic differences between the two documents and delivers a prioritized action plan for developing the Baylor Performance Playbook into a best-in-class departmental training and SOP manual. Additionally, it outlines a standalone Intern Sport Science Curriculum aligned with the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook.

### Key Findings

The Baylor document is a solid operational foundation but is significantly less comprehensive than the Clemson model. The primary gaps fall into five categories:

No intern/GA curriculum or educational programming structure

No sport-specific data dictionaries (the current data dictionary is generic/vendor-level, not contextualized to Baylor sports)

Missing daily operational checklists, schedules, and accountability structures

Technology workflows are generic and template-like rather than Baylor-specific with step-by-step detail

No guiding principles, policies, or professional development framework for staff and interns

## SECTION 2: STRUCTURAL COMPARISON

The following table maps the major sections of each document to highlight what exists, what is missing, and what needs development.

## SECTION 3: DETAILED CRITIQUE OF THE BAYLOR OPERATIONS GUIDE

### 3.1 Strengths

Strong institutional framing: The Preparing Champions for Life mission and One Standard/One Accord values provide a meaningful organizational identity that Clemson lacks.

Health & Wellness ecosystem: The inclusion of Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services missions establishes Applied Performance within the broader support structure.

ForceDecks data dictionary depth: The jump metric glossary (take-off phase, landing phase metrics) is more technically detailed than Clemson's equivalent.

Perch VBT metric explanations: The 3D position, velocity, and power calculation breakdowns are well-written and educationally valuable.

Hyperlinked resources: External links to vendor user manuals and test guides add value without bloating the document.

### 3.2 Weaknesses & Gaps

#### 3.2.1 Identity and Purpose

The Baylor document reads more like a vendor product reference manual than a departmental playbook. The Clemson document tells you who they are, what they do, and why it matters before presenting any technology. The Baylor version jumps from institutional mission directly into technology with very little connecting tissue explaining how Applied Performance operates day-to-day.

#### 3.2.2 Technology Workflows

The VALD DynaMo, ForceFrame, NordBord, Perch, Polar, and SmartSpeed workflows all follow an identical template structure (Preparation, Participant Registration, Device Calibration, Testing Protocol, Positioning, Conducting the Test, Data Collection, Feedback, Post-Test, Data Export). While organized, this template-driven approach has several problems:

It reads like it was generated from a generic template rather than written from practitioner experience at Baylor.

There are no Baylor-specific device names, serial numbers, storage locations, or account details.

There is no troubleshooting section for any device (Clemson includes troubleshooting for every technology).

The Catapult workflow is the only one with genuine operational detail; the others need the same treatment.

#### 3.2.3 Data Dictionary

The current data dictionary is organized by technology vendor (Catapult parameters, Perch parameters, ForceDecks parameters, Polar parameters) rather than by sport. This means a staff member working with soccer cannot quickly find all the metrics relevant to their team. Clemson organizes their data dictionary by sport (Baseball, Men's Soccer, Volleyball, etc.) and lists only the technologies and metrics used by each sport. This is far more actionable for coaches and performance staff.

#### 3.2.4 Missing Operational Infrastructure

The following operational elements are entirely absent from the Baylor document:

Daily intern/GA checklist with device charging and readiness protocols

Social media and student-athlete interaction policies

Intern/GA schedule and semester learning objectives

Professional expectations and conduct standards

Data management and reporting pipelines (where does data go after collection?)

Credential and password management protocol

Equipment maintenance schedule and inventory tracking

#### 3.2.5 Educational and Development Components

The Clemson Playbook doubles as a training manual. It includes a 173-page intern curriculum with slide-deck-style educational content covering the fundamentals of sports science, force plates, GPS, force-velocity profiling, heart rate monitoring, data hygiene, data visualization, soft skills, research methods, sports medicine, and strength & conditioning. The Baylor document has no educational component whatsoever. Any intern or new staff member receiving the Baylor document would know how to set up devices but would not understand why they are doing so or how the data fits into the bigger picture.

## SECTION 4: PRIORITIZED ACTION PLAN

The following action plan is organized into three phases based on impact and effort.

### Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1–4)

High-impact, relatively low-effort additions that immediately improve the document's utility.

Draft an Applied Performance Introduction section that explains who the team is, what interns/GAs can expect, and daily responsibilities.

Create a Policies section covering social media, student-athlete interactions, confidentiality, and professional conduct.

Build a Daily Operations Checklist with device inventory, charging protocols, pre-session setup, and post-session teardown tasks.

Expand the Operating Principles from bullet format to narrative descriptions with practical examples.

Establish a credential management protocol (e.g., shared 1Password vault) and document the process in the Playbook.

### Phase 2: Operational Depth (Weeks 5–10)

Moderate-effort improvements that transform the document from a reference guide into a true operational playbook.

Rewrite all technology workflows with Baylor-specific details: device names/serial numbers, storage locations, account credentials (referenced via vault), step-by-step procedures written from practitioner experience, and troubleshooting guides.

Create sport-specific data dictionaries for each team supported by Applied Performance, listing only the technologies and KPIs relevant to that sport with contextualized threshold values.

Develop a data management pipeline section documenting the flow from data collection through storage (Kitman Labs, VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud), analysis, visualization, and reporting.

Add an Equipment Inventory and Maintenance section with serial numbers, purchase dates, warranty info, and maintenance schedules.

Create reporting templates and dashboards section showing examples of weekly/monthly reports for coaching staffs.

### Phase 3: Education & Culture (Weeks 11–16+)

Higher-effort additions that elevate the Playbook into a comprehensive training and development resource.

Develop the standalone Intern Sport Science Curriculum (see Section 5 below).

Create an Intern/GA Semester Schedule with weekly topics, learning objectives, deliverables, and presentation milestones.

Build a Professional Development section with networking expectations, conference attendance, social media best practices, and career pathway guidance.

Add case studies and applied practice scenarios for each technology/sport combination to bridge the gap between data collection and decision-making.

Establish a version control and review cycle (e.g., annual review each May with updates before fall semester).

## SECTION 5: INTERN SPORT SCIENCE CURRICULUM FRAMEWORK

The following outlines a standalone 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum designed to be a separate document from the Performance Playbook. It is aligned with the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook and adapted from the Clemson model to reflect Baylor's technology stack, organizational structure, and operational philosophy.

### 5.1 Curriculum Philosophy

The curriculum is built on the principle that interns must understand both the why and the how of applied sport science. Each week combines conceptual education (readings, lectures, discussions) with hands-on technical training (device operation, data collection, analysis). Interns should leave the program with a portfolio of work and the confidence to operate independently in a collegiate sport science environment.

### 5.2 Semester Schedule

### 5.3 Key Differences from the Clemson Curriculum

While the Clemson curriculum provides an excellent template, the Baylor version should be adapted in several important ways:

Technology alignment: Clemson's curriculum references 1080 Sprint, Proteus, Moxy, MuscleLab, PlyoMat, and GymAware, none of which are in Baylor's current stack. The Baylor curriculum should center on ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, and Polar.

Sport context: Clemson's examples lean heavily on Olympic sports (soccer, volleyball, rowing, softball, baseball, track). Baylor should incorporate football-specific examples alongside Olympic sport contexts given the department structure.

Standalone format: Clemson embeds the curriculum inside the Playbook as slide decks. Baylor should create a separate, dedicated curriculum document that can be distributed independently and updated on its own cycle.

Assessment and portfolio: Add formal intern assessment rubrics and require a portfolio of work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics) that interns can use professionally.

Integration with Health & Wellness: Baylor's unique structure (Applied Performance within Health & Wellness) should be reflected in the curriculum by including sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health Services.

### 5.4 Intern Project Requirements

Each intern should complete a semester-long project that demonstrates applied competency. Suggested project categories:

Sport-specific dashboard: Build a weekly or monthly reporting dashboard for one Baylor sport using real (de-identified) data.

Technology validation: Conduct a reliability or validity study on a Baylor technology using appropriate statistical methods.

Literature review and infographic: Summarize the current evidence on a sport science topic and translate it into a practitioner-facing infographic.

Data integration project: Combine data from two or more sources (e.g., GPS + force plates + wellness) and present an integrated analysis.

## SECTION 6: RECOMMENDED FINAL PLAYBOOK STRUCTURE

Based on this analysis, the completed Baylor Performance Playbook should follow this structure:

Note: The Intern Sport Science Curriculum should be maintained as a separate standalone document that references the Playbook but can be distributed and updated independently.

## SECTION 7: NEXT STEPS

To move from this plan to execution, the following immediate next steps are recommended:

Review this document and prioritize which Phase 1 items to tackle first based on upcoming semester needs.

Assign ownership for each Playbook section (e.g., who writes the Catapult workflow vs. the ForceDecks workflow).

Determine the target completion date for each phase (suggest: Phase 1 complete before fall semester, Phase 2 by mid-fall, Phase 3 by end of fall).

Decide on the Intern Curriculum delivery format: separate PDF, slide decks, or a combination.

Identify 2–3 sports to pilot the sport-specific data dictionaries and use them as templates for the rest.

Establish a shared workspace (e.g., Google Drive folder, SharePoint site) for collaborative editing of the Playbook.

<!-- page 26 -->
WHY DO SPORTS SCIENTISTS USE 
FORCE PLATES AND MOTION CAPTURE?
 Objective measures of athlete movement behavior and strategies
 Generally high reliability → sensitive to physiological change due to 
injury, stress, fatigue, etc.
 Major technological advancements → easy to assess athletes in a 
large university setting
133

<!-- page 27 -->
CURRENT STATE OF FORCE PLATES 
AND MOTION CAPTURE
 Force plates
 Portable (collegiate / professional settings)
 Embedded (research setting)
 Motion capture
 Markerless (collegiate / professional settings)
 Markered (research setting)
134

<!-- page 28 -->
HOW DO FORCE PLATES WORK?
 Provide information on kinetics (the study of force applied to and by 
objects)
 Forces measured via strain gauges, piezoelectric cells, or load cells
 Acceleration, velocity, power, and displacement can be derived from 
force plate data
 Flight-time (e.g., jump height) and impulse-momentum 
(neuromuscular strategy) metrics can be derived
John Harry – Texas Tech 
135

<!-- page 29 -->
FORCE PLATE ASSESSMENTS
 Isometric assessments
 Mid-thigh pull
 Squats, leg press, upper body 
assessments
 Peak force and rate-of-force 
development
 Dynamic assessments
 Counter-movement jump, squat-jump, 
drop-jump
 Performance and injury-based 
assessments
 Reactive strength index, joint moments 
calculations
Richter, Betancur, Taberner (NSCA, 2022)
136

<!-- page 30 -->
HOW DOES MOTION CAPTURE WORK?
 Provide information on kinematics (the study of motion independent 
of the forces that cause motion)
 Motion capture measured via 2D/3D cameras and IMU technology
 Position-velocity-acceleration (linear and angular outcomes)
 3D motion capture is the gold standard (inverse dynamics to 
determine joint moments)
NSCA, 2022
137

<!-- page 31 -->
TECHNICAL CONSIDERATIONS WITH 
FORCE PLATES AND MOTION CAPTURE
 Force plates
 Mechanical “ringing” (high frequency oscillations)
 Filtering techniques (raw vs filtered data)
 May perform a power spectrum analysis (set 
sampling frequency based on this)
 No consensus, just maintain consistency!
 Motion capture
 Physiological “noise” (motion artifacts due to 
clothing, skin tissue)
 Filtering and gap-filling techniques
 Lighting and calibration quality
Abolins, 2017
139

<!-- page 32 -->
CONTACT GRIDS
 What are they?
 Infrared light or switch mat technologies that detect when an athlete 
contacts the ground
 What outcomes do they capture?
 Contact time = time spent on ground per ground contact
 Jump height = converted from flight time
 RSI = flight time / contact time
 Limb asymmetry

HOW DO GPS UNITS WORK?
 Acts as receivers to determine location, velocity, and time
 GPS units interact with satellites at the velocity of light
 Require at least 4 satellites to determine physical location (latitude and 
longitude)
 Sampling frequency = rate that GPS units receives satellite signals
 Initial units sampled at 1 Hz, newer devices sample at 10 Hz
 Outcomes: x- and y-coordinates transformed into time-motion 
analysis

 Total Player Load
 Sum of accelerations across all axes (scaling factor for comparisons)
 Measure of exertion not dependent on distance

 VHSD = total distance covered over 15 mph
 HSD = total distance covered over 11.8 mph
 VHSD Exposures
 Number of sprints over 15 mph (> 2 seconds)
 A3 / D3
 Total accelerations greater than 3 m/s2 and decelerations less than -3 m/s2
 …many others (e.g., total swings, total jumps)

 Positional differentiation = determines change in device location over 
time
 Doppler-shift method = determines rate of change in satellite signal 
frequency caused by receiver movement to calculate velocity
 Greater precision for velocity calculation (accuracy of cm / sec)
 GPS units typically determine distance through positional 
differentiation and velocity though Doppler-shift method

WHY IS FORCE-VELOCITY PROFILING 
IMPORTANT IN SPORTS SCIENCE?
 Change in direction (speed up or slow down) or velocity (acceleration 
or deceleration) is determined by force application
 Force is dependent on movement velocity
 Power = force x velocity
Morin & Samozino, 2016
166

<!-- page 50 -->
FORCE-VELOCITY-POWER PROFILING
 To determine F-V or P-V relationships, the athlete must perform an 
assessment at different velocities executed maximally
167

<!-- page 51 -->
NONSPECIFIC AND SPECIFIC F-V-P
 Nonspecific (e.g., jumping)
 Vertical profiling
 Force production in the same orientation as the limb
 Specific (e.g., sprinting)
 Horizontal profiling
 Force production not in the same orientation as the limb
168

<!-- page 52 -->
NONSPECIFIC STRENGTH 
MEASUREMENT METHODS
 Range-of-motion standardization
 Starting position (e.g., lowest position of 
CMJ) can be pre-determined (give knee 
angle) or freely chosen by the athlete 
(preferred option)
 Reliability
 Require 4 – 6 progressive loading 
(resistance) conditions to cover the largest 
range of velocities
 Range of velocities covered by the different 
conditions is more important than the 
number of conditions
169

<!-- page 53 -->
SPORT-SPECIFIC STRENGTH 
MEASUREMENT METHODS
 Gold standard assessments
 Force-embedded tracks / treadmills 
(sprinting) and pedals (cycling)
 Load conditions
 Typically corresponds to % of body weight
 Reliability
 To cover the largest range of velocities 
possible, peak sprint velocity should be 
reached within 5 – 6 sec
 Outcomes
 Provides force production and orientation 
quality (mechanical effectiveness)
170

KEY F-V-P METRICS (NONSPECIFIC)
 Pmax = maximal power output
 Most macroscopic dynamic strength measure
 Similar Pmax may be achieved by 2 athletes with different strength profiles 
(force production at low versus high velocities)
 SFV = ratio between the theoretical force and velocity maximum
 Independent from Pmax

<!-- page 55 -->
KEY F-V-P METRICS (SPORT-SPECIFIC)
 Pmax, Fo, Vo, SFV = describe very similar mechanical features
 Sprint-specific force production in the horizontal direction
 RF = ratio of horizontal force to resultant force over a step
Dorn, 2012

 Biggest confounder

 Biggest confounder

VARIABILITY

<!-- page 59 -->
HEART RATE
 First introduced into sports in 1983
 Heart rate = number of heart beats per minute
 Heart rate variability (HRV) = variation in beat-to-beat intervals over a 
specified time
 No gold standard exists for HR monitoring to calculate training load
176

<!-- page 60 -->
HEART RATE REGULATION
 Tightly controlled feedback loops regulate and maintain 
energy homeostasis
 Autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and 
parasympathetic systems)
 Sympathetic system
 Physical stressor (training)
 Environmental stressors (temperature)
 Psychological stressors (anxiety)
 Internal conditions (hydration)
 Parasympathetic system acts to restore homeostasis 
after periods of stress
177

<!-- page 61 -->
HEART RATE MONITORING
 Explosion in wearable technology to monitor HR
 2 main categories
 Electrical (ECG) - detect electrical signals, greater accuracy at higher 
intensities
 Optical (photoplethysmography) – detect blood flow changes
178

<!-- page 62 -->
MEASURING HEART RATE
 Resting HR
 Reflects changes in acute and chronic fatigue
 Standardization is VERY important for data interpretation
 Time of day, body position, nutrition
 HR during exercise
 Greater variation due to multidimensional physiological conditions
 24-hr HR
 More practical with wearables
 Requires further validation
179

<!-- page 63 -->
MEASURING HEART RATE VARIABILITY
 General indicator of health, wellness, and fitness
 Requires additional data processing
 Current best practices = measure HRV between 3 – 5 minutes under 
standardized environmental conditions
 Obtain 3 – 4 measurements / week
180

<!-- page 64 -->
CALCULATING HEART RATE VARIABILITY
 Time-domain = variability in time differences between R-R intervals
 Most suitable for applied settings
 Power spectral analysis = measures frequency of R-R interval changes and 
bins 3 categories
 Low-frequency power
 Very low-frequency power
 High-frequency power
181

<!-- page 65 -->
CALCULATING HEART RATE VARIABILITY
 Root mean square of successive differences between normal heartbeats 
(RMSSD)
 Most widely reported and used HRV measure
182

<!-- page 66 -->
TRAINING LOAD USING HR MEASURES
 HR > 100 – 110 bpm are largely driven by the sympathetic nervous system
 HR% of HRmax = gauge of relatively intensity
 Higher HR = greater sympathetic activity and anaerobic energy contributions
NSCA, 2022
183

<!-- page 67 -->
TRAINING IMPULSE
 TRIMP helps quantify training intensity and volume
 Generally requires:
 Time
 HR zone
 HR max
 HR rest

<!-- page 68 -->
MONITORING CHANGES IN FITNESS & FATIGUE
 HR and HRV provide the response to training / competition
 To make data actionable, external / internal parameters are required
 GPS data
 RPE metrics
 Sleep
 Travel
 Stress
185

<!-- page 69 -->
ACUTE HR RESPONSE
 Volume and intensity are the 2 biggest influencers
 Intensity is more influential on sympathetic activity
 High-intensity = 48 hr recovery
 Moderate intensity = 24 – 48 hr recovery
 Low intensity = 24 hr recovery
 Heart rate recovery = how quickly HR decreased following exertion
 Withdrawal of sympathetic input > reactivation of parasympathetic system
 Approx. 60 sec of recovery needed
186

WHY ARE RESEARCH METHODS &

SCIENCE?
 Quantify the relationship between

strategies to determine these 
relationships
 Critically evaluate current / future 
practices
248

<!-- page 121 -->
RESEARCH DESIGN IN SPORTS 
SCIENCE
 Descriptive / observational
 Case study
 Cross-sectional
 Cohort / prospective / longitudinal
 Case-control / retrospective
 Experimental
 Randomized control trial
 Crossover
 Blinded
249

<!-- page 122 -->
DESCRIPTIVE / OBSERVATIONAL 
STUDIES
 Observe athletes without providing an intervention
 Case study – Reports data on a single athlete or few athletes
 Used for unique cases
 Provides greater insight compared to group-based studies
 Typically, not generalizable
 Cross-sectional – Athletes are assessed at a single time point
 Most time efficient study design for group-based studies
 Provides “snapshot” of performance that may be influenced by many 
factors
250

<!-- page 123 -->
DESCRIPTIVE / OBSERVATIONAL 
STUDIES
 Longitudinal / prospective – Repeatedly examine the same athletes to 
detect any changes over time
 Careful planning prior to study initiation
 Much stronger study design than cross-sectional
 May offer a naturalistic observation 
 Case-control / retrospective – Uses data that had previously been 
collected
 Case control – cases with and without the condition are identified and 
compared (e.g., ACL vs non-ACL injured athletes)
 Generally considered inferior to prospective study designs
251

<!-- page 124 -->
EXPERIMENTAL STUDIES
 Provide athletes a specific intervention
 Randomized control trial – “Gold standard” research study
 Athletes randomly assigned to experimental or control groups
 Provides greater insight compared to group-based studies
 Typically, not generalizable
 Blinded – Athletes are unaware of which group they were placed in
 Removes “placebo effect”
 Single-blind = athletes are blinded
 Double-blind = athletes and researchers are blinded
 Crossover – Interventions are crossed-over during the study time 
period
252

<!-- page 125 -->
DATA TYPES
 Nominal scale (categorical)
 Distinct classes w/o a quantitative value
 Example: sport (baseball, softball, tennis, etc)
 Ordinal scale
 Implied order with unknown distance
 Example: RPE scale (1 – 10)
 Interval scale
 Implied order with known distance (no true zero)
 Example: temperature (degrees Fahrenheit)
 Ratio scale
 An interval scale with a true zero
 Example: height, weight, velocity
253

<!-- page 126 -->
STATISTICAL MODELING
 Description
 Summarize and describe data
 We do this very well!
 Prediction
 Applying a statistical model to “predict” 
new or future events
 We need to do this more often!
 Causal inference
 Drawing a conclusion about a causal 
connection
 Very rare in our environment
 NSCA, 2022
254

<!-- page 127 -->
DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS
 Describe data without making predicative or causal claims
 Most common examples
 Comparing independent groups
 Comparing dependent groups
255

<!-- page 128 -->
DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS
 Central tendency measures
 Mean (average)
 Mode
 Median (useful for non-normal distributions)
 Spread measures
 Standard deviation
 Interquartile range
 Min, max, and range
 Skewness (asymmetry)
 Kurtosis (tail heaviness – outliers)
NSCA, 2022
256

<!-- page 129 -->
MEAN AND EFFECT SIZE
 Mean
 Simplest statistical model
 Heavily influenced by sample size and outliers
 Root mean square error
 Determines the accuracy of a statistical model 
versus observed data
 Lower RMSE = better fit
 Effect size
 Strength or magnitude between variables or 
groups
 Cohen’s d = most popular in sports science
 Common Language Effect Size (CLES)
NSCA, 2022
257

<!-- page 130 -->
ASSOCIATION BETWEEN VARIABLES
 Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient
 Measures strength of linear relationship between 2 
variables
 Range: -1 to +1 (0 – no relationship, -1/+1 perfect 
relationship)
 R2 = variance explained between variables
 Linear regression is the underlying statistical model 
of correlations
NSCA, 2022
258

<!-- page 131 -->
CORRELATION ≠ CAUSATION
 Be aware of potential confounders
 A variable that influences both the dependent and independent variables
 These may be difficult to identify
 Random sampling helps eliminate confounders
 Linear regression is the underlying statistical model of correlations
259

<!-- page 132 -->
NULL-HYPOTHESIS SIGNIFICANCE 
TESTING
 Sample data is tested against a null hypothesis 
(Ho)
 No effect/differences between or among groups
 Often tested based upon a pre-defined p-value
 p-value = the probability of obtaining data assuming 
the null hypothesis is correct
 p-values may be heavily influenced by research 
practices
P-hacking practices
260

<!-- page 133 -->
ONE- AND TWO-SIDED SIGNIFICANT 
TESTING
 One-sided approach used when there 
is certainty about the direction of the 
effect
 Two-sided approach used when the 
expected direction of the effect is 
unknown
 More conservative, typically used for 
preliminary analysis
NSCA, 2022
261

<!-- page 134 -->
TYPE 1 & TYPE 2 ERRORS
 Type 1 error – rejecting the null hypothesis when the null is true
 Alpha (α)
 Type 2 error – rejecting the alternative hypothesis when the 
alternative is true
 Beta (β)
 Statistical power = 1 - β
 More willingness to make Type 1 errors, the less likeliness to 
make Type 2 errors (vice versa)
262

<!-- page 135 -->
STATISTICAL INTERPRETABILITY
 The degree to which a human can understand the cause of a decision
 High interpretability = means, linear regression
 Low interpretability = machine learning, neural networks
 Understand your target audience when developing statistical models
VS

 Validity = The degree to which a test or device 
measures what it claims to measure
 Criterion = Relationship to a gold standard 
assessment technique
 Construct = Applies when there is not a criterion 
measure (e.g., athlete training load)
 Reliability = The consistency of a measure, often 
determined through test-retest
 A test or device cannot be valid if it is not 
reliable!
264

MEASUREMENT STUDIES
 Measurement error – observed value 
differences from the true value
 Measurement “noise”
 Instrumentation – Error due to device 
 Example: Uncalibrated force plates
 Biological – Error due to physiological processes
 Examples: Sleep deprivation, neuropsychological 
effects
 Systematic – Stable error across all 
measurements (bias)
 Random – Unpredictable error that varies 
between measurements
265

67	Specific Tests vs. General Tests
68	
69	Sport-specific tests have utility with the assessment process, but rarely is the strength & conditioning
70	
71	coach grading or assessing such processes. Typically, the goal of the Strength & Conditioning
72	
73	Coach is to utilize more general tests that provide some of the underpinning determinants
74	
75	of such specific tasks in sports.
76	
77	An example is a vertical jump seen in Basketball and Volleyball. The vertical jump
78	
79	outcomes may be similar across athletes, but the underpinnings of vertical jump relate to the impulse
80	
81	(Force x Time). So, an athlete would need to demonstrate the ability to express maximal force production ability and demonstrate the ability to develop force rapidly. Tests of the Back Squat and/or Deadlift for maximal strength, and test of ballistic exercises such as cleans, snatches, jump squats for explosive strength
82	
83	may provide a clearer picture of where an athlete needs to spend time to enhance vertical jump performance.

85	## Validity
86	
87	A valid test measures what it is intended to measure (and is considered suﬃciently reliable to use).
88	
89	### Types of validity
90	
91	### Construct: refers to the overall validity, or the extent to which the test measures what it is designed to measure.
92	
93	### Face: is the appearance to the athlete, coach, and other practitioners that the test measures what it is purported to measure.
94	
95	### Content: refers to the expert assessment that the monitoring tool measures what it claims to measure.
96	
97	### Criterion: refers to the relationship between the scores on the test and scores on a criterion measure. Criterion measure is a test that is widely accepted as a gold-standard and valid test—E.g. Force plates for force testing vs. deriving force from a displacement sensor (e.g., Gymaware).
98	
99	## Reliability
100	
101	The reliability of a measure (test) can be viewed simply as the amount of variation that occurs from one test occasion to another.
102	
103	### Types of Reliability
104	
105	### Interrater reliability: refers to the degree to which different people conducting the assessment agree on their test results over time or on repeated occasions.
106	
107	### Interrater reliability: refers to the consistency of scores in repeated tests conducted by a single tester.
108	
109	## Detecting Change
110	
111	## The sensitivity of an assessment (or even a monitoring) tool refers to its ability to detect small but significant changes in performance or an aspect such as fatigue.
112	
113	## Meaningful change is defined as the smallest practical change that is important.
114	
115	Reassessment
116	
117	Reassessment is primarily dependent upon three factors:
118	
119	Time within the competition year. There is a contextual evaluation that must occur to ensure the proper placement of assessments. This is significantly more important the closer one is to the competition period.
120	
121	The expectation of change. If you are in a maximal strength phase for a beginner or intermediate athlete, you may consider reassessing in 4 weeks. If the athlete is an advanced athlete, you may consider a more extended period. This is also dependent upon the length of the phase. The length of the training period would extend the reassessment date to allow for adequate recovery to occur.
122	
123	Unexpected recovery issues. Do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue. A big reason for reassessment is to provide the athlete the confidence they are improving. Ensure their readiness matches their assessment needs. This may require multiple assessment dates for a team sport or a larger group of individuals. Be flexible

166

326

334

391	most powerful assessment tools that offer insight into the success of the development of your

Baylor University Athletics

Performance Assessment Manual

Table of Contents

Why Assessments?

Validity

Types of Validity

Reliability

Types of Reliability

Detecting Change

Performance Assessments determined by the sport

Common Assessments Descriptions

Power

Why Assessments?

Specific Tests vs. General Tests

Sport-specific tests have utility with the assessment process, but rarely is the strength & conditioning

coach grading or assessing such processes. Typically, the goal of the Strength & Conditioning

Coach is to utilize more general tests that provide some of the underpinning determinants

of such specific tasks in sports.

An example is a vertical jump seen in Basketball and Volleyball. The vertical jump

outcomes may be similar across athletes, but the underpinnings of vertical jump relate to the impulse

(Force x Time). So, an athlete would need to demonstrate the ability to express maximal force production ability and demonstrate the ability to develop force rapidly. Tests of the Back Squat and/or Deadlift for maximal strength, and test of ballistic exercises such as cleans, snatches, jump squats for explosive strength

may provide a clearer picture of where an athlete needs to spend time to enhance vertical jump performance.

## Validity

A valid test measures what it is intended to measure (and is considered suﬃciently reliable to use).

### Types of validity

### Construct: refers to the overall validity, or the extent to which the test measures what it is designed to measure.

### Face: is the appearance to the athlete, coach, and other practitioners that the test measures what it is purported to measure.

### Content: refers to the expert assessment that the monitoring tool measures what it claims to measure.

### Criterion: refers to the relationship between the scores on the test and scores on a criterion measure. Criterion measure is a test that is widely accepted as a gold-standard and valid test—E.g. Force plates for force testing vs. deriving force from a displacement sensor (e.g., Gymaware).

## Reliability

The reliability of a measure (test) can be viewed simply as the amount of variation that occurs from one test occasion to another.

### Types of Reliability

### Interrater reliability: refers to the degree to which different people conducting the assessment agree on their test results over time or on repeated occasions.

### Interrater reliability: refers to the consistency of scores in repeated tests conducted by a single tester.

## Detecting Change

## The sensitivity of an assessment (or even a monitoring) tool refers to its ability to detect small but significant changes in performance or an aspect such as fatigue.

## Meaningful change is defined as the smallest practical change that is important.

Reassessment

Reassessment is primarily dependent upon three factors:

Time within the competition year. There is a contextual evaluation that must occur to ensure the proper placement of assessments. This is significantly more important the closer one is to the competition period.

The expectation of change. If you are in a maximal strength phase for a beginner or intermediate athlete, you may consider reassessing in 4 weeks. If the athlete is an advanced athlete, you may consider a more extended period. This is also dependent upon the length of the phase. The length of the training period would extend the reassessment date to allow for adequate recovery to occur.

Unexpected recovery issues. Do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue. A big reason for reassessment is to provide the athlete the confidence they are improving. Ensure their readiness matches their assessment needs. This may require multiple assessment dates for a team sport or a larger group of individuals. Be flexible

Team Cultures and Assessments

There will be several specific and even general assessments that you may likely never do because they are already happening within sports practice already. This doesn't necessarily mean you dismiss the assessments, but you can use their information to help triangulate what you're seeing to come up with possible valuable insight to the athlete and coaching staff. Additionally, you may be in a situation where several testing elements are mandated by the coaching staff. In order to determine if improvements in performance are occurring, establish objective criteria by which the test can be assessed if none exists.

## Baylor Sport Assessment Table

General Assessments

Movement screen (Fusionetics)

Description:

Fusionetics is the tool used for the assessment of movement dysfunction through a series of bilateral and unilateral exercises. Each exercise is scored by a practitioner based on a specific set of criteria. Based on the score, a diagnosis of movement dysfunction is made, and a specific corrective exercise program is designed.

Frequency of testing:

There should be a minimum of ONE time per year where this assessment should be performed. The most impactful time(s) is when your student-athletes have been away from campus for an extended period and/or after the competition season.

Anthropometrics

Description:

Anthropometrics have a strong association with success for most sports. There

are certain heights, weights, and muscle to fat ratios that appear to help optimize performance outcomes.

Frequency of Testing:

Height:

Bodyweight: Individual team protocols

Body composition No more than 4x / year

Jump Assessments

Counter Movement Jump (Various hand positions)

Description:

The countermovement jump (CMJ) offers a lot of insight into the athlete's performance abilities by itself, when used in combination with other tests, and is a helpful tool to gauge compensatory patterns (when using the force plate), and can be a valid tool to monitor

neuromuscular fatigue.

How to Test:

Hands-on hips CMJ:

Stand on the jump mat or force plate with hands-on-hips.

Instruct the athlete to simply jump as high as possible. Do not coach the strategy of jumping.

Have athletes perform 2-3 jumps.

Hands-free CMJ:

Stand on the jump mat or force plate with hands at the side.

Instruct the athlete to simply jump as high as possible. Allow the athlete to angulate at the shoulder; arms come behind the body and extend upwards as the athlete projects vertically. Do not coach the strategy of jumping.

Have athlete perform 2-3 jumps.

Frequency of testing:

Jump Height:

Weekly or Before and after training phases, it depends on your purpose. If you are going weekly, you will want to utilize the AVERAGE jump height across 2 – to 3 jumps

Equipment:

Contact Mat (only for Jump Height)

Broad Jump

Description: The broad jump offers a lot of insight into the athlete's performance abilities by itself. The primary being the athlete's ability to express power horizontally, along with assessing movement compensation and alterations to jumping and landing strategies

How to Test:

The athlete stands behind a line marked on the ground with feet slightly apart. A two-foot take-off and landing are used, with the swinging of the arms and bending of the knees to provide forward drive. The subject attempts to jump as far as possible, landing on both feet without falling backward.

Frequency of Testing:

Jump Height: Weekly or Before and after training phases; it will depend on your purpose.

Equipment:

Measuring tape and ruler

Weighted Throw

Standing or Side Medicine Ball Throw

Description: This test measures upper and lower body strength and explosive power, particularly with a twisting action

How to Test:

The subject stands at a line with the feet slightly apart and facing the direction the ball is to be thrown. Start with the hands held just under the ball, the arms extended in front of the body. The ball is then swung back behind the body, twisting the hips and torso, then swung back vigorously to throw the ball out as far as possible. Encourage the subject to use the legs, back, and arms to assist in maximizing the distance thrown; the subject is also permitted to fall forward over the line after the ball is released. The action is repeated on each side of the body, and three attempts are allowed on each side.

Frequency of Testing:

Before and after training phases

Equipment:

Medicine Ball and Measure tape

Maximal Strength Assessments

1 RM Estimation - Maximal Strength

Description:

For maximal strength determination, practitioners are getting away from performing 1RM attempts in the weight room primarily due to its risk and the subsequent cause of undue fatigue that may negatively hinder performance for multiple days after, especially if there is a significant emotional component during the lift. The alternate is velocity-based 1RM estimation. This is performed with a linear displacement transducer (Gymaware) attached to the barbell while the athlete performs one repetition for multiple loads. Once the efforts are completed, linear regression is used to estimate the 1RM.

How to Test:

After the athlete finishes some lightweight warm-up repetitions, begin with roughly a 50% load. This load and all subsequent loads must be done with the same eccentric tempo with a maximal concentric phase. The average repetition velocity (m/s) and weight will be recorded.

Continue taking roughly 10% increments until you reach 85-90% loads or when the athlete reaches around 0.1-0.15+ of the associated mean velocity at 1RM below.

Associated Mean Velocity at 1 RM

Squat & Variations: 0.3 m/s

Bench & Variations: 0.2 m/s

Power Hang Snatch & Variations: 1 m/s

Power Hang Clean & Variations: 0.8 m/s

Frequency of Testing:

Before and after your training phases to gauge how much development has occurred.

Suppose the athlete is performing their lifts with the GymAware device every week. In that case, you can gauge a relatively accurate representation of how 1RM performance is changing without waiting until your training phases are completed.

Equipment:

Gymaware

Repetition Maximum

Various Repetition Protocols

Description:

For maximal strength, determination practitioners can use a variety of repetition protocols to determine an athlete's projected 1 repetition maximum (1RM)

3RM Protocol:

The participant should perform a warm-up with a self-selected load that allows them to complete a minimum of 6-10 repetitions (approx. 50% predicted 1RM).

1-5-minute rest

Participants then select a weight based on the previous effort, which allows them to perform 3-repetitions

1-minute rest

Participants then select a weight based on the previous effort, which allows them to perform 3-repetition.

The test has concluded when an athlete has arrived at a weight, and they can no longer safely perform for 3 repetitions

5RM: Protocol:

The participant should perform a warm-up with a self-selected load that will allow them to complete a minimum of 6-10 repetitions (approx. 50% predicted 1RM).

1-5-minute rest

Participants then select a weight based on the previous effort, which allows them to perform 5-repetitions

1-minute rest

Participants then select a weight based on the previous effort, which allows them to perform 5-repetitions.

The test has concluded when an athlete has arrived at a weight, and they can no longer safely perform for 5 repetitions

Frequency of Testing:

At the end of a training block, where appropriate to assess gains in maximal strength

Equipment:

1RM estimation formula

1RM = weight x (1 + (reps / 30))

Endurance Assessments

Yo-Yo Level 1 or 2 Intermittent Test

Description:

The yo-yo intermittent recovery test (Yo-Yo IRT) is utilized because it has been viewed as a valid and reliable estimate of aerobic endurance, is efficient and straightforward to administer and has been sufficiently researched and validated with many different sports.

How to Test:

Measure out 25m on a zero-slope pitch/field/court

Place markers at the 0m line, 5m line, and 25m line.

The 0-5m zone is the walking zone. 5-25m is the running zone

To start the test, it is best to utilize an audio track that has been designed with the appropriate speed tempo, rest, and incremental speed adjustments. You'll need a smartphone and speaker for this.

The athlete continues each stage until they fail to cross the line before the end of the stage.

Yo-Yo IRT1 starts at a lower speed and has smaller increments in speed than the Yo-Yo IRT2.

Yo-Yo IRT1 is used to determine an athlete's individual endurance capacity; this may be

better suited to younger athletes.

Yo-Yo IRT2 is used to determine the capacity of an athlete to recover from repeated exercise that requires a high contribution from the anaerobic systems

If an athlete can run faster than speed level 23 on Yo-Yo IRT1, they should perform the Yo-Yo IRT2 on the next occasion.

Frequency of Testing:

This type of assessment is usually done at the beginning of longer training phases and usually is employed before the pre-competition phases.

Interpretation of Results:

If you want to estimate VO2Max, you can use the test results

Yo-Yo IRT1 distance (m) x 0.0084 + 36.4

Yo-Yo IRT2 distance (m) x 0.0136 + 45.3

Equipment:

Cones, an audio file, speaker

Repeat Sprint Ability (RSA)

Description: The Repeat Sprint Ability assessment gauges the efficiency of repeated neuromuscular efforts. This is particularly useful in sports with periods where there are several high-intensity sprinting efforts with short periods of rest between them. This test offers two primary elements: To gauge the sprinting time across 20-30 meters and to gauge the decrement of performance over subsequent sprint efforts

How to Test:

After a proper warm-up, the athletes are to run 6, 20-30m sprints with 30 seconds of rest between efforts.

Times for all sprints are gathered.

Frequency of Testing:

Within training, weekly

Assess at the end of a training phase

Interpretation of Results:

Ideal time(s) = Best time x 6

Decrement (%) = (Total / Ideal) x 100

Generally, you're looking for a decrement between 2-10%.

If greater than 10%, you may consider having the athlete perform aerobic-based training. If less than 10%, you may consider having the athlete perform speed-based training.

Speed Assessments

Linear Sprinting

Description:

Linear sprinting with highly sensitive and reliable timing equipment is one of the

most powerful assessment tools that offer insight into the success of the development of your

locomotive athletes. When you perform the test with multiple distances, you can effectively

identify where an athlete may need to speed more time in their development.

How to Test:

To ensure higher reliability, team sport athletes should utilize a 2-point start.

Instruct the athlete to self-select their start vs. initiating via your command.

Have them run maximally for 30-40 meters.

Have them perform at least 2 sprints.

Frequency of Testing:

Since most programs have sprinting built into their training, the frequency can be as frequent as you train. But there is a clear difference between training and testing, so to effectively gauge test-to-test improvements, ensure you are not relying on training data if you have previous testing data.

If you do not measure during training, perform testing before and after training phases.

Interpretation of Results:

0-10m is considered their acceleration score

If you are working more on maximal strength, power, and slow SSC development, you should predictably see this phase improve.

30-40m is considered their speed score

If you are working more on sprinting and fast SSC development, you should predictably see this phase improve.

0-40m is their combined

40m peak velocity (m/s) - take the 30m split time and subtract it from the 40m split time and decide by 10 for this value.

Equipment:

SmartSpeed

• Jump Height (Flight Time) – Jump Height calculated from Flight Time; in centimeters (cm) 
• Jump Height (Flight Time) in Inches – Jump Height (Flight Time) converted to inches; in inches (in) 
• Jump Height (FT) Relative Landing RFD – Landing RFD divided by Jump Height (Flight Time); in Newtons per second per 
centimeter (N/s/cm) 
• Jump Height (FT) Relative Peak Landing Force – Peak Landing Force divided by Jump Height (Flight Time); in Newtons per 
centimeter (N/cm) 
• Lower-Limb Stiffness – Change in Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase divided by Countermovement Depth; in Newtons 
per meter (N/m) 
• Mean Eccentric+Concentric Power:Time – Mean Power between Start of Movement and Take-off, divided by Contraction 
Time; in Watts per second (W/s) 
• Minimum Eccentric Force – Minimum Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase; in Newtons (N) 
• Movement Start to Peak Force – Time Period between Start of Movement and the point when Peak Vertical Force occurs 
prior to Take-off; in seconds (s) 
• Movement Start to Peak Power – Time Period between Start of Movement and the point when Peak Power occurs prior to 
Take-off; in seconds (s) 
• P1 Concentric Impulse – Net Impulse during the first 50% of the Concentric Phase (time-wise); in Newton seconds (N s) 
• P2 Concentric Impulse – Net Impulse during the second 50% of the Concentric Phase (time-wise); in Newton seconds (N s) 
• P2 Concentric Impulse:P1 Concentric Impulse – Ratio of P2 Concentric Impulse to P1 Concentric Impulse; unitless 
• Peak Net Take-off Force / BM – Maximum Vertical Force between Start of Movement and Take-off, - Body Weight, and divided 
by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg) 
• Peak Power – Maximum Power during the Concentric Phase; in Watts (W) 
• Peak Power / BM – Peak Power divided by Body Mass; in Watts per kilogram (W/kg)

<!-- page 27 -->
20 
 
 
• Peak Take-off Acceleration – Maximum Acceleration of the Center of Mass between Start of Movement and Take-off; in 
Meters per second squared (m/s2) 
• Positive Impulse – Net Impulse during the entire repetition (eccentric, concentric, and landing combined); in Newton seconds 
(N s) 
• Positive Take-off Impulse – Net Impulse during Take-off (eccentric and concentric phases combined); in Newton seconds (N 
s) 
• RSI-modified – Jump Height (Flight Time) divided by Contraction Time; in meters per second (m/s) 
• RSI-modified (Imp-Mom) – Jump Height (Imp-Mom) divided by Contraction Time; in meters per second (m/s) 
 
Landing Phase Metrics 
• Jump Height (Imp-Dis) – Maximum Displacement of the Center of Mass between Take-off and Landing; in centimeters (cm) 
• Jump Height (Imp-Mom) – Jump Height calculated from the Velocity of the Center of Mass at the instant of Take-off and Body 
Mass; in centimeters (cm) 
• Jump Height (Imp-Mom) in Inches – Jump Height (Imp-Mom) converted to inches; in inches (in) 
• Landing Impulse – Absolute Impulse from Landing to the point when Peak Landing Force occur; in Newton seconds (N s) 
• Landing Net Peak Force / BM – Maximum Vertical Force after Landing, - Body Weight, and divided by Body Mass; in Newtons 
per kilogram (N/kg) 
• Landing RFD – RFD between Landing and the point when Peak Landing Force occurs; in Newtons per second (N/s) 
• Landing RFD 50ms – RFD of the first 50ms following Landing; in Newtons per second (N/s) 
• Mean Landing Power – Average Power between Landing and the end of the rep; in Watts (W) 
• Peak Landing Acceleration – Maximum Acceleration of the Center of Mass between Landing and the end of the rep; in meters 
per second squared (m/s2) 
• Peak Landing Force – Maximum Vertical Force after Landing; in Newtons (N) 
• Peak Landing Force / BM – Peak Landing Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg) 
• Peak Landing Power – Maximum Power between Landing and the end of the rep; in Watts (W) 
• Peak Landing Velocity – Maximum Velocity of the Center of Mass between Landing and the end of the rep; in meters per 
second (m/s) 
• Take-off Peak Force – Maximum Vertical Force between Start of Movement and Take-off; in Newtons (N) 
• Take-off Peak Force / BM – Take-off Peak Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg) 
• Time to Braking Phase – time period between Start of Movement and the beginning of the Eccentric Braking Phase;  in 
seconds (s) 
• Total Work – Integration of Power (i.e., area under the Power-Time curve) between Start of Movement and Take-off; in Joules 
(J) 
• V elocity at Peak Power – Velocity of the Center of Mass at the point when Peak Power between Start of Movement and Take -
off occurs; in meters per second (m/s) 
• Vertical Velocity at Take-off – Velocity of the Center of Mass at the point when Take-off occurs; in meters per second (m/s)

 Oxidative – Long-term, low intensity 
activities
 Duration: Greater than 3 min
 Sands, Wurth, & Hewit
324

<!-- page 164 -->
SPECIFIC ADAPATATIOS TO 
IMPOSED DEMANDS (SAID)
 An athlete’s body will adapt to exact demands placed upon it
 All training is specific to some outcome
 Example: biceps curls will not make you run faster!
325

<!-- page 165 -->
OVERREACHING & 
OVERTRAINING
NSCA, 2022
 Inappropriate combinations of training volume, intensity, and 
frequency may lead to increased fatigue and decreased 
recovery
 Delicate balance between applied training stress and 
recovery
326

<!-- page 166 -->
TRAINING ORGANIZATION
 Annual plan / Macrocycle – Organization of training for the entire 
calendar year
 Mesocycle – Intermediate training duration lasting weeks to a few 
months
 Microcycle – Short-term training duration lasting one to a few weeks 
(e.g., tapering period)
MACROCYCLE
1 YEAR

MICROCYCLES
INDIVIDUAL TRAINING SESSIONS

Selye, 1956 & 1974

EXERCISE SELECTION AND 
TRAINING PRESCIPTION
Sands, Wurth, & Hewit
329

<!-- page 169 -->
PLYOMETRICS
 Jumping exercises to train power, rate of force development, 
and force attenuation qualities
 3 phases
 Eccentric – lengthening of agonist muscle tissue
 Amortization – time delay between the eccentric pre-stretch and 
force generation of the muscle contraction
 Concentric – shortening of agonist muscle tissue
330

<!-- page 170 -->
STRETCH-SHORTENING CYCLE 
(SSC)
 Underlying physiological tissue response during plyometric 
activities
 Force, work, and power output during shortening phase is 
enhanced by pre-stretch compared to conditions with a pre-
stretch
Seiberl, 2021

change of velocity or direction in

movement jump performance in the rowing team. One rower asks, 
“Why can’t I jump as high during the squat jump?”

Testing Protocol

Testing can be performed under the following conditions.

Condition 1: Performing tests within a training session

Condition 2: Performing tests outside of a training session

Standard Warm up:

Line hops (Forward/Backward/Left/Right) x 10 each

Open gate/Close gate (Hip internal/external rotation) x 5 each

Rapid Squat to Stand (Triple Extension) x 5 each

Testing Order:

Test Protocol/Procedure:

Hands Free Body Weight Squat:

Starting position:

standing posture.

Arms extended out from the shoulder keeping them fixed for each rep.

Feet shoulder width apart.

ForceDecks protocol:

Ask individual to assume starting position.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight.

Stabilize individual – Instruct the individual to remain completely still, for 2-3 seconds before, and between each rep.

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform squat rep then resume the starting position.

Repeat squat for desired number of reps.

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Squat Jump:

Starting position:

Partial squat position / quarter-squat position.

Hands on hips.

Chest up and looking forward.

ForceDecks protocol:

Assume starting position – Ask individual to assume starting position.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight.

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform jump - Instruct the individual to:

Lower into a squat position above parallel depth.

Hold position, keeping chest up and hands on hips, for 3 seconds.

Jump up.

Land softly.

Assume starting position again.

Repeat jump for desired number of reps.

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Countermovement Jump

Starting position:

Normal standing posture.

Hands on hips (if unweighted) or hands on barbell (if weighted).

Chest up and looking forward.

ForceDecks protocol:

Assume starting position – Ask the individual to assume starting position on the plates.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform jump – Instruct the individual to:

Keep the chest up and looking forward.

Bend down.

Jump up.

Land softly.

Assume starting position again.

Repeat jump total of 3 countermovement jumps.

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Hop Test (Repeated CMJ Test)

Starting position:

Normal standing posture.

Hands on hips.

Chest up and looking forward.

ForceDecks protocol:

Assume starting position – Ask individual to assume starting position.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight.

Stabilize individual – Instruct the athlete/client to remain completely still, in the standing position for 2-3 seconds before the first jump.

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform jump – Instruct the individual to:

Keep chest up and looking forward.

Bend down.

Jump up.

Land stiff-legged on only the toes.

Quickly jump off the toes, for the desired number of reps, in rapid succession (safely keeping the knees as straight as possible).

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Single Leg Countermovement Jump

Starting position:

Normal standing posture.

Hands on hips (if unweighted) or hands on barbell (if weighted).

Chest up and looking forward.

ForceDecks protocol:

Starting position – Ask the individual to assume starting position on the plates.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform single leg jump – Instruct the individual to:

Keep the chest up and looking forward.

Bend down using only the desired leg for testing.

Jump up using only the desired leg for testing.

Land softly using only the desired leg for testing.

Assume starting position again.

Repeat jump for a total of 3 countermovement jumps each, per leg.

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Isometric Seated Calf Raise:

Starting position:

Assume a seated position.

Feet flat at the approximate center of the platform.

Ankle directly under the knee (90 deg position at the knee and ankle).

Place belt/strap approximately a palm width away from the top of the knee.

ForceDecks protocol:

Select “Mid-Thigh Pull” from exercise testing menu.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight.

Ask individual to assume starting position as described above.

Make sure there is pre-tension through the ankle.

Once belt/strap is in place, no more than a fingertip should fit under.

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Instruct individual to:

Drive maximally with the ball of the foot into the platform.

Maintain contraction for 6 seconds or when instructed to “relax”.

Rest for 15 seconds between reps.

Perform 3 maximal contraction reps.

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

| Squat Jump | x3 |

| Countermovement Jump | x3 |

6	
7	Most performance staff have been there. You implement a new monitoring tool, build the workflow around it, get buy-in from coaches, and wait for the insights to roll in.  Months later, you're staring at a dataset that tells you almost nothing you can trust.
8	
9	That was our experience with daily wellness questionnaires.
10	
11	In the summer of 2022, we rolled out wellness across multiple sports at Baylor, delivered directly to athletes through our AMS app. The premise was sound: subjective readiness data, collected daily, to inform training decisions. We committed fully and collected data for the better part of a full academic year.

Most performance staff have been there. You implement a new monitoring tool, build the workflow around it, get buy-in from coaches, and wait for the insights to roll in.  Months later, you're staring at a dataset that tells you almost nothing you can trust.

That was our experience with daily wellness questionnaires.

In the summer of 2022, we rolled out wellness across multiple sports at Baylor, delivered directly to athletes through our AMS app. The premise was sound: subjective readiness data, collected daily, to inform training decisions. We committed fully and collected data for the better part of a full academic year.

The problem surfaced within three months. Athletes weren’t refusing to participate; they were complying, just not honestly. The scores were consistent, the responses were on time, and the data were mostly useless. Athletes had learned the pattern and answered accordingly. By the end of the first semester, it was clear across several teams that little genuine thought was going into the responses. The surveys had become a box-checking exercise rather than a real snapshot of readiness.

The problem with subjective wellness data is that it requires something objective doesn’t, it requires the athlete to be an accurate and honest narrator of their own state. That’s a significant ask in a college environment where athletes are managing academic pressure, social stress, and a natural tendency to tell coaches what they want to hear.

We already had force plates in our program, using CMJ testing to track longitudinal performance trends. The next logical step was to leverage mRSI as a daily readiness marker. The force plates didn’t ask athletes how they felt, it just measured what was there. Objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quire were.

That said, we haven’t written wellness monitoring off entirely. We still use surveys in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context fills gaps that objective data cannot. But as a daily, large-scale collection tool, the return wasn’t there.

Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it’s time to stop collecting.

There are tests that make complete sense in theory but fall apart the moment you try to scale them. Nordic hamstring testing was that for us, and the reason we stopped had nothing to do with the test itself.

We stopped using the NordBord for roster-wide monitoring because we couldn't consistently collect enough data to make it meaningful. Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data.

The Nordbord is a legitimate tool. The research behind eccentric hamstring strength and injury risk is well established, and the metrics it produces are valid. When we began collecting with our Football program in January 2023, the intent was sound. Build a hamstring strength profile across the roster, track it over time, and use it to inform training and return-to-play decisions.

The reality of doing that with 120-plus athletes and a single unit looked very different.

Each session took 25 to 30 minutes to work through a group. Scaled across an entire roster, with position-group scheduling, practice obligations, and other off-field commitments competing for the same time windows, consistent collection became almost impossible. We'd get a solid block of testing, then lose weeks before we could test again.

That’s the hidden cost of a logistically demanding test; it doesn't just slow you down, it creates large gaps in your data. Longitudinal monitoring only works when data points are comparable. When gaps appear, you stop tracking change and start collecting disconnected snapshots that are difficult to act on.

Staff turnover at the end of the spring season accelerated the decline. In the transition, the planning and coordination required to execute testing at scale quietly stopped being prioritized. Without someone owning the process, it didn’t survive the off-season.

We still use the Nordbord, just differently. In return-to-play scenarios with a smaller, targeted group of athletes, paired with joint-specific isometric testing, it earns its place. Smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight. That’s an environment where you can control the conditions well enough for the data to mean something.

The lesson wasn’t about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful. Good data requires consistent collection, and consistent collection requires systems that can survive staff changes, schedule pressure, and the daily demands of a Power 4 program. When those systems aren’t in place, even a valid test stops being valuable.
